So the pattern is: one MERGE that closes changed current rows and inserts genuinely new customers, then a follow-up INSERT that creates the new current version for whatever just got closed.

The join condition is doing real work here -- matching only on customer_id plus is_current = 1 means we're always comparing against the one current row, never accidentally re-triggering off old history. I'd also flag that the change-detection condition needs to handle NULLs carefully in a real system; a plain <> comparison against a NULL value never evaluates to true in SQL, so if segment can be NULL and changes from NULL to an actual value, this would silently miss that as a 'no change' unless you wrap it in ISNULL or use IS DISTINCT FROM-style logic.

And I'd wrap the whole two-statement sequence in an explicit transaction, because if the MERGE commits and closes a row but the second INSERT fails before creating its replacement, you've got a customer with zero current rows, which breaks every downstream join expecting exactly one current row per customer.
commonMistakes: Trying to force both the close and the new-row insert into a single MERGE WHEN MATCHED clause
Matching the MERGE join on customer_id alone without restricting to is_current = 1, which can re-trigger against historical rows
Using a plain <> comparison for change detection without handling NULLs
Not wrapping the two-statement pattern in a transaction, risking a customer left with zero current rows
Forgetting the NOT EXISTS idempotency guard, risking duplicate current rows if the batch reruns
keyPoints: SCD Type 2 requires two physical operations per change (close old, insert new) that one MERGE cannot both perform
Join predicate must restrict to the current row (is_current = 1) to avoid matching historical rows
Change detection must be NULL-safe across all tracked attributes
A follow-up INSERT keyed off newly-closed rows creates the new current version
An idempotency guard (NOT EXISTS) protects against duplicate current rows on reruns
The two statements should run in one transaction to avoid leaving a customer with zero current rows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why one MERGE cannot fully express SCD Type 2
SQL correctly closes changed rows and inserts new/current rows with correct join predicates
Addresses NULL-safe change detection
Addresses idempotency and transactional safety
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Choosing and Configuring a dbt Incremental Strategy for a Multi-Billion-Row Fact Table
questions.prompt: A fact_events model ingests roughly 400 million new rows per day into a table that already holds several billion rows, and late-arriving data can update events up to 3 days after they first land. Write the dbt model config for an incremental strategy that handles this correctly and efficiently, and explain why a naive append-only incremental strategy would silently produce duplicate or stale rows given the late-arrival pattern.
questions.modelAnswer:
A naive 'append' incremental strategy -- insert only rows with a timestamp greater than the max timestamp already in the table -- assumes every event is written exactly once and never revisited, which breaks the moment late-arriving data can update an event up to 3 days after it first lands: if event X lands on day 1, and an update to event X arrives on day 3, a plain append strategy's WHERE clause (`updated_at > max(updated_at) already loaded`) will indeed pick up the day-3 update row, but 'append' means it gets inserted as a brand-new row alongside the original -- producing a duplicate event_id in the table rather than replacing the original with its updated version. Any downstream aggregation that doesn't explicitly dedupe on event_id now double-counts that event.

The `merge` incremental strategy fixes this by using unique_key (event_id here) to perform a real upsert: for each incoming row, if a row with that event_id already exists in the target, its columns get updated in place rather than a second row being inserted; if it doesn't exist, it's inserted as new. That's what correctly handles the late-arriving-update case -- the day-3 update to event X overwrites the day-1 row for the same event_id instead of duplicating it.

The remaining piece is making sure the late-arriving rows are actually included in what gets selected for the incremental run at all -- a merge strategy only helps with rows that are actually in this run's result set. If the model's filter only looks at rows strictly newer than yesterday's max event_date, a 3-day-late update to an old event would never even be selected for reprocessing, merge or not. That's why the incremental filter reprocesses a trailing window (here, 4 days back from the current max event_date) rather than a single-day cutoff -- wide enough to cover the known late-arrival pattern, while partitioning and clustering on event_date keep that bounded re-scan efficient at billions-of-rows scale instead of requiring a full-table scan every run.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The failure mode I'd flag immediately is what a plain append strategy does with that 3-day late-arrival pattern: it'll happily pick up the late update because its filter is just 'anything newer than what I've already loaded,' but 'append' means inserting, not updating -- so the late row for an event that already exists becomes a second row with the same event_id, not a correction of the first one. Every downstream count or sum now double-counts that event unless someone remembers to dedupe, which defeats the point of an incremental model being correct on its own.

Switching to merge with unique_key set to event_id fixes that specific problem -- now when the late row comes through, dbt generates a real upsert, so it overwrites the existing event_id's row instead of adding a duplicate.

But I'd also point out that merge alone doesn't save you if your filter never selects the late row in the first place. If the incremental WHERE clause only grabs 'since yesterday,' a correction to an event from three days ago never even enters this run's result set, so merge never gets a chance to apply it. That's why I widen the filter to a trailing window -- four days back, matching the known late-arrival pattern -- so the model deliberately re-scans a bounded recent slice every run instead of assuming yesterday's data is already final. And I'd partition and cluster on event_date specifically so that wider re-scan stays cheap even with billions of rows already in the table, instead of degrading into a full scan.
commonMistakes: Using an append-only incremental strategy for data with any late-arrival/update pattern
Assuming unique_key/merge alone fixes correctness without also widening the incremental selection filter
Filtering the incremental run on a single-day cutoff instead of a trailing window matching the known late-arrival lag
Not partitioning/clustering by the date field used in the trailing-window filter, causing expensive re-scans at scale
Forgetting on_schema_change handling, risking a failed run when the source adds a new column
keyPoints: Append-only incremental strategies cannot handle late-arriving updates to already-loaded rows
merge with unique_key performs a real upsert, overwriting the existing row instead of duplicating it
A merge strategy only helps for rows actually included in the incremental selection filter
The filter must use a trailing window matching the known late-arrival lag, not a single-day cutoff
Partitioning/clustering by the filtered date column keeps the trailing-window re-scan efficient at scale
on_schema_change should be configured deliberately rather than left to fail on upstream schema drift

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why append-only strategies fail under late-arriving updates
Correctly configures merge strategy with unique_key
Correctly widens the incremental filter to a trailing window matching the lag
Addresses partitioning/clustering for efficiency at scale
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Configure an Idempotent Kafka Producer with a Dead Letter Queue for Poison Pills
questions.prompt: Write Python producer/consumer configuration (using confluent-kafka or kafka-python style config) for a pipeline that must not create duplicate messages on retry, and must route a message to a dead letter topic instead of blocking the whole partition when that message repeatedly fails to process. Explain what each key config does.
questions.code:
from confluent_kafka import Producer, Consumer, KafkaError

producer_conf = {
    'bootstrap.servers': 'broker1:9092,broker2:9092',
    'enable.idempotence': True,   # turns on producer ID + per-partition sequence numbers
    'acks': 'all',                 # required with idempotence; waits for full ISR ack
    'max.in.flight.requests.per.connection': 5,  # safe up to 5 with idempotence on
    'retries': 2147483647,          # retry indefinitely; idempotence prevents duplicate writes
    'delivery.timeout.ms': 120000,
}
producer = Producer(producer_conf)

dlq_producer = Producer(producer_conf)

consumer_conf = {
    'bootstrap.servers': 'broker1:9092,broker2:9092',
    'group.id': 'order-events-processor',
    'enable.auto.commit': False,   # commit only after successful processing
    'auto.offset.reset': 'earliest',
}
consumer = Consumer(consumer_conf)
consumer.subscribe(['order-events'])

MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3

def process(msg):
    attempts = 0
    while attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS:
        try:
            handle_event(msg.value())  # business logic; idempotent on event_id
            return True
        except TransientError:
            attempts += 1
    # poison pill: route to DLQ instead of blocking this partition forever
    dlq_producer.produce(
        'order-events-dlq',
        key=msg.key(),
        value=msg.value(),
        headers=[('original_topic', msg.topic().encode()),
                 ('failure_reason', b'max_retries_exceeded')],
    )
    dlq_producer.flush()
    return False

while True:
    msg = consumer.poll(1.0)
    if msg is None or msg.error():
        continue
    process(msg)
    consumer.commit(msg)  # commit only after process() handled success or routed to DLQ
questions.modelAnswer:
The producer side's job is preventing duplicates on retry, and `enable.idempotence: True` is the setting that actually does that: it assigns the producer a unique ID and tags every message with a monotonically increasing per-partition sequence number, so if a retry resends a message the broker already committed, the broker recognizes the repeated sequence number and silently discards the duplicate instead of appending it again. Idempotence requires `acks=all` (so the producer only considers a write successful once it's fully replicated) and caps `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` at 5 for correctness guarantees to hold with modern brokers, which is why those three settings travel together rather than being independent choices. Setting `retries` very high is safe specifically because idempotence is on -- without it, aggressive retrying would just create more duplicates, not fewer.

The consumer side's job is not letting one bad message (a poison pill -- malformed payload, a business-logic exception that will never succeed no matter how many times it's retried) block every message behind it on the same partition forever. `enable.auto.commit: False` matters here because committing only after `process()` actually returns is what prevents silently acknowledging a message that was never successfully handled -- auto-commit on a timer could advance the offset past a message that's still mid-processing or that failed, causing silent data loss rather than a retry.

The retry-then-DLQ pattern inside `process()` gives a message a bounded number of attempts to succeed (covering genuinely transient failures like a brief downstream outage) before conceding it's a poison pill and routing it, with failure context in headers, to a dead letter topic -- and only then committing the original offset. That's the mechanism that keeps the partition moving: instead of the consumer looping forever on one message (or crashing and restarting into the exact same message repeatedly), the DLQ absorbs the message that genuinely cannot be processed, and processing continues on everything behind it. Someone -- an on-call engineer, an automated reprocessor -- can later inspect the DLQ, fix the root cause, and replay those messages deliberately.
questions.professionalAnswer:
On the producer side, the setting doing the actual work is enable.idempotence -- that's what stops a retry from becoming a duplicate. It gives the producer an ID and a per-message sequence number, so if the ack gets lost and the producer retries, the broker's already seen that exact sequence number and just drops the repeat instead of writing it twice. I'd flag that this isn't a standalone setting -- turning it on requires acks=all and caps in-flight requests at 5, so those three go together, and that's also why I'm comfortable setting retries to effectively unlimited here -- normally that'd worry me, but with idempotence on, retrying aggressively doesn't cost you duplicates anymore.

On the consumer side, the thing I'd always build in from day one is the DLQ pattern, because the alternative -- one malformed message that will never successfully process, sitting there being retried forever -- takes down the whole partition behind it. I turn off auto-commit specifically so I control exactly when an offset advances: only after process() either succeeds or has given up and shipped the message to the DLQ. That way a crash mid-processing doesn't silently skip a message, and a message that's never going to succeed doesn't block everything behind it either.

The retry count before giving up is a judgment call based on how long genuinely transient failures in your downstream usually last -- I used 3 here, but the real point is drawing a clear line between 'this might just be a blip, try again' and 'this is never going to work, get it out of the critical path and let someone look at it later.'
commonMistakes: Enabling retries without enabling idempotence, which multiplies duplicates instead of preventing them
Using auto-commit, which can advance the offset past a message that failed or is still processing
Not having any DLQ mechanism, letting one unprocessable message block the entire partition
Not distinguishing transient errors (worth retrying) from permanent/poison-pill errors (route to DLQ)
Forgetting to preserve failure context (headers) when routing to the DLQ, making later reprocessing harder
keyPoints: enable.idempotence uses producer ID + sequence numbers so retries don't create duplicate writes
Idempotence requires acks=all and bounded max.in.flight.requests.per.connection
High retry counts are safe only because idempotence prevents them from becoming duplicates
Manual offset commits (auto-commit off) prevent silently acknowledging unsuccessfully processed messages
A bounded retry count distinguishes transient failures from permanent poison-pill failures
DLQ routing keeps the partition moving past a message that can never succeed, enabling later manual reprocessing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly configures and explains idempotent producer settings
Correctly explains manual offset commit timing and why it matters
Correctly implements a bounded retry-then-DLQ pattern
Code is syntactically plausible and internally consistent
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Design a Reusable Terraform Module for a Data Platform Landing Zone
questions.prompt: Write a Terraform module skeleton (variables, resources, outputs) for a per-environment 'landing zone' that provisions a storage account/bucket, a least-privilege service identity scoped to it, and resource tags for cost attribution -- parameterized so the same module stands up dev, test, and prod with different sizing and access policies. Explain the design choices that make it safely reusable across environments rather than copy-pasted per environment.
questions.modelAnswer:
The reusability comes from pushing every environment-specific decision into variables with environment-appropriate defaults, rather than writing three nearly-identical copies of the module for dev/test/prod. The `environment` variable's validation block is doing real work, not just documentation -- it fails the plan immediately with a clear error if someone passes a typo'd environment name, instead of silently provisioning a resource with a nonsense name or tag. `replication_type` defaulting to LRS (locally redundant, cheapest) but being overridable per environment in that environment's own .tfvars file lets prod opt into GRS (geo-redundant) without the module itself needing an if/else per environment hardcoded into the resource block -- the module stays generic, and environment-specific risk tolerance lives in environment-specific configuration, which is exactly where it's easiest to review and audit.

The identity is deliberately scoped with `azurerm_role_assignment` at the storage-account level (`scope = azurerm_storage_account.landing.id`), not at the resource-group or subscription level, which is the least-privilege principle made concrete: this identity can only touch this one storage account, so a credential leak or a misconfigured pipeline using this identity has a blast radius limited to this landing zone, not the whole environment's infrastructure. Using a user-assigned managed identity rather than a service principal with a stored secret also removes a credential that could leak from CI logs or a secrets store entirely.

Tagging via a single `local.common_tags` map applied consistently to every resource is what makes cost attribution actually work later -- FinOps reporting that groups spend by cost_center or environment tag only works if every resource in the module carries the same tag keys with consistent values, which centralizing them in one local block guarantees, versus each resource block setting tags ad hoc and drifting out of sync over time. The net effect is that calling this module three times with three different .tfvars files (dev.tfvars, test.tfvars, prod.tfvars) produces three environments that are structurally identical but independently sized, isolated, and tagged -- which is both safer and far easier to review in a PR than three hand-maintained near-duplicate resource blocks.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The design goal here is that nobody should ever need to copy this module's code to add an environment -- they should only ever need a new .tfvars file. That's why almost every environment-specific decision -- replication type, sizing, who owns it -- is a variable with a sensible default rather than something baked into the resource block itself. The validation block on the environment variable is a small thing but it's saved me real debugging time before: it fails fast and loud if someone typos 'staging' instead of 'test,' instead of quietly creating a resource with a weird name that someone finds confusing six months later.

The identity scoping is the part I'd call out as the actual security decision in this module: that role assignment is scoped to this one storage account's resource ID, not the resource group, not the subscription. So if this specific identity's credentials ever leak -- through a bad CI log, a misconfigured pipeline -- the damage is contained to this one landing zone. I'd also point out it's a user-assigned managed identity, not a service principal with a client secret sitting in a vault somewhere, which removes an entire category of credential-leak risk.

And the tagging -- I always centralize that into one local map applied to every resource, because the moment tags are set ad hoc per resource, they drift, and then whoever's trying to build a cost-attribution report six months from now finds three different capitalization variants of the same cost center and has to clean it up by hand. One map, applied everywhere, keeps that report trustworthy without anyone having to think about it again.
commonMistakes: Hardcoding environment-specific values (replication type, sizing) into the resource block instead of variables
Scoping the identity's role assignment at the resource-group or subscription level instead of the specific resource
Using a service principal with a stored secret instead of a managed identity
Setting tags ad hoc per resource instead of centralizing them, causing cost-attribution drift
Skipping input validation on variables like environment, allowing silent typos to provision mis-tagged resources
keyPoints: Environment-specific decisions live in variables with defaults, not hardcoded per-environment branches
Input validation on key variables (e.g., environment) fails fast on typos instead of silently misconfiguring
Least-privilege: role assignment scoped to the specific resource, not the resource group or subscription
Managed identity avoids storing a service-principal secret anywhere
Centralized tag map ensures consistent cost attribution across every resource the module creates
Same module code produces structurally identical, independently configured environments via separate tfvars

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Module design correctly parameterizes environment-specific behavior via variables
Correctly scopes the identity/role assignment for least privilege
Centralizes tagging for consistent cost attribution
Includes meaningful input validation
Clear, accurate explanation of reusability design choices

questions.title: Build an Airflow DAG That Orchestrates dbt on Top of a Cross-Platform Ingestion Step
questions.prompt: Write an Airflow DAG (TaskFlow API style) that: 1) waits for a cross-platform ingestion job (e.g., a Fivetran/Airbyte sync or a Kafka Connect sink) to finish, 2) triggers a dbt build scoped to the models that depend on that source, and 3) sends an alert on failure without retrying indefinitely. Explain why triggering dbt from Airflow is preferable to relying on dbt Cloud's own standalone job scheduler for this specific scenario.
questions.modelAnswer:
The sensor task's job is to make the dbt build's start condition explicit and observable rather than guessed by a fixed time offset -- a common anti-pattern is scheduling dbt to run 'at 6:30am, an hour after ingestion usually finishes,' which silently breaks the first time ingestion runs long. Using `mode='reschedule'` instead of the default poke mode matters at any real scale, because reschedule releases the worker slot between polls instead of holding it busy-waiting, which avoids a long-running sensor from starving the worker pool other tasks need.

The bounded `retries=2` plus a fixed `retry_delay`, combined with explicitly raising `AirflowFailException` the moment the sensor detects the upstream connector itself reported 'failed' (rather than just timing out and retrying blindly), is the key design choice for 'alert without retrying indefinitely': a transient blip (ingestion still running, a brief API hiccup checking status) gets a bounded number of automatic retries, but a definitive upstream failure fails fast instead of burning an hour of retry delay before anyone's paged. The `alert_on_failure` task's `trigger_rule='one_failed'` is what wires the alert without needing a separate on_failure_callback on every task -- it only runs if something upstream in the DAG actually failed, and stays dormant on a clean run.

Triggering dbt from Airflow instead of relying on dbt Cloud's own standalone scheduler is the right call here specifically because the real dependency isn't time, it's a cross-platform data-readiness event -- dbt needs to not start until the Fivetran/Airbyte/Kafka Connect sync has actually finished successfully, and dbt Cloud's own scheduler has no native way to know that happened; it can only run on a cron-like schedule, which reintroduces the exact 'hope ingestion finished by then' guesswork the sensor exists to eliminate. Airflow is the right home for this logic because it's the orchestrator that already has (or can be given) visibility into the ingestion tool's actual job status via its API/provider, letting the dbt run's trigger condition be genuinely data-driven -- 'the source data actually landed' -- rather than schedule-driven.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The sensor at the top is doing more work than it looks like -- it's replacing a guess ('ingestion is probably done by 6:30') with an actual check against the ingestion tool's real status. I'd specifically use reschedule mode here rather than the default poke mode, because poke mode holds a worker slot busy the entire time it's waiting, and if ingestion runs long some mornings, that's a worker slot other DAGs needed, sitting idle doing nothing but checking a status flag.

The failure handling is deliberately asymmetric: if the sensor sees the upstream connector actually reported failed, I raise immediately rather than letting it keep polling and eventually time out -- that's the difference between paging someone in two minutes versus an hour. Genuinely transient issues, like a flaky status-check API call, still get the normal bounded retries, but a real failure doesn't get to hide behind retry logic. And the alert task's trigger_rule of one_failed means I don't have to wire a failure callback onto every single task -- it just fires if anything upstream actually failed, and does nothing on a clean run.

As for why this lives in Airflow instead of letting dbt Cloud schedule itself: dbt Cloud's scheduler is fundamentally time-based, it has no native concept of 'wait until this Fivetran sync actually finishes.' The real dependency here isn't a clock, it's an event -- data has to actually land before dbt should touch it -- and Airflow is the tool that can see both sides of that: the ingestion tool's status and dbt's own run. Scheduling dbt on its own clock just reintroduces the exact race condition this whole DAG exists to avoid.
commonMistakes: Scheduling dbt at a fixed time offset after ingestion instead of waiting on an actual completion signal
Using sensor poke mode instead of reschedule mode, holding worker slots busy unnecessarily
Letting a definitive upstream failure retry blindly instead of failing fast with an explicit exception
Wiring a separate failure callback on every task instead of a single trigger_rule='one_failed' alert task
Relying on dbt Cloud's own scheduler for a dependency that is event-driven, not time-driven
keyPoints: Sensor task makes the dbt build's start condition an actual data-readiness check, not a time guess
reschedule mode avoids holding a worker slot busy during a long wait
Bounded retries handle transient issues; explicit failure exceptions handle definitive upstream failures fast
trigger_rule='one_failed' centralizes failure alerting without per-task callbacks
dbt Cloud's own scheduler cannot natively wait on a cross-platform ingestion tool's completion event
Airflow is the right home for this logic because it can see both the ingestion tool's and dbt's status

evaluationCriteria.criterion: DAG correctly waits on ingestion completion rather than a fixed schedule offset
Correctly implements bounded retries with fast-fail on definitive failure
Correctly implements centralized failure alerting
Correctly explains why Airflow, not dbt Cloud's scheduler, should own this trigger
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Build a Snowflake Streams + Tasks Pipeline for Near-Real-Time CDC Propagation
questions.prompt: Write Snowflake SQL that uses a stream on a raw landing table plus a scheduled task to incrementally propagate change data (inserts, updates, deletes) into a curated table, without reprocessing rows that have already been propagated. Explain what the stream actually tracks and why the task must consume the stream's offset in the same transaction as its DML to avoid losing or duplicating changes.
questions.code:
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM raw.orders_stream ON TABLE raw.orders
  APPEND_ONLY = FALSE;  -- capture inserts, updates, deletes, not just appends

CREATE OR REPLACE TASK curated.propagate_orders
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
  SCHEDULE = '5 MINUTE'
WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('raw.orders_stream')
AS
MERGE INTO curated.orders AS tgt
USING (
  SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, status, metadata$action, metadata$isupdate
  FROM raw.orders_stream
) AS src
  ON tgt.order_id = src.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND src.metadata$action = 'DELETE' AND NOT src.metadata$isupdate THEN
  DELETE
WHEN MATCHED AND src.metadata$action = 'INSERT' AND src.metadata$isupdate THEN
  UPDATE SET tgt.customer_id = src.customer_id, tgt.amount = src.amount, tgt.status = src.status
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND src.metadata$action = 'INSERT' THEN
  INSERT (order_id, customer_id, amount, status)
  VALUES (src.order_id, src.customer_id, src.amount, src.status);

ALTER TASK curated.propagate_orders RESUME;
questions.modelAnswer:
A Snowflake stream doesn't store the changed rows themselves -- it stores an offset into the source table's change tracking metadata (backed by the table's underlying versioned micro-partitions), and a query against the stream computes the delta between that offset and the table's current state on the fly, exposing it with METADATA$ACTION ('INSERT' or 'DELETE') and METADATA$ISUPDATE (true when a row's change represents an update, which Snowflake internally represents as a paired delete-then-insert of the same key) columns. APPEND_ONLY=FALSE is what makes the stream capture updates and deletes, not just new rows, which this use case requires since the raw table isn't insert-only.

The offset only actually advances when a DML statement consumes the stream inside a transaction that also commits -- querying a stream in a SELECT alone, without a subsequent DML statement in the same transaction that consumes it (like the MERGE here), does not advance the offset. That's the mechanism that makes this safe to run on a schedule without losing or duplicating changes: the task's MERGE statement both reads the stream's current delta and, as part of committing that same transaction, advances the stream's offset past the rows it just consumed. If the task's MERGE fails partway and the transaction rolls back, the offset does not advance either, so the same unconsumed changes are still there, correctly, for the next scheduled run to pick up -- nothing is lost. If the offset advanced independently of whether the MERGE's changes actually committed, a failed run could either silently skip rows (offset moved forward, but the MERGE's changes were rolled back) or require manual reconciliation; coupling them in a single transaction is what prevents both failure modes.

The `WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA(...)` task condition is a cost-saving detail, not a correctness requirement -- it skips actually starting the warehouse and running the MERGE on a schedule tick when the stream has no pending changes, which matters because Snowflake tasks otherwise consume warehouse credits just to check and find nothing to do.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The mental model I'd give someone new to this is: the stream isn't a queue of saved rows, it's a bookmark. It remembers an offset into the source table's own change history, and every time you query it, Snowflake computes 'what's changed since that bookmark' on the fly using the table's internal versioning -- it's not physically storing a copy of every changed row somewhere. METADATA$ACTION and METADATA$ISUPDATE are how it tells you what kind of change each row represents, including that Snowflake models an update internally as a delete paired with an insert on the same key, which is why the MERGE logic needs to check both flags together to tell a true delete apart from an update.

The part that actually matters for correctness is when that bookmark moves. It only advances when some DML statement reads from the stream and that statement's transaction actually commits -- just querying the stream with a plain SELECT doesn't move it. So by writing the MERGE as the thing that both consumes the stream and commits, I've tied 'did we apply the changes' and 'did we advance the bookmark' into one atomic unit. If the MERGE fails and rolls back, the bookmark doesn't move either -- so nothing's lost, the next run just sees the same pending changes again. If those two things weren't coupled in one transaction, you'd risk the nightmare scenario of the bookmark advancing even though the actual data changes never got applied, which silently drops data with no error to alert you.

The stream-has-data check on the task is really just a cost optimization -- there's no point spinning up the warehouse and running a MERGE every five minutes if nothing's actually changed, so that condition skips the run entirely when the stream's empty.
commonMistakes: Believing a stream physically stores copies of changed rows rather than an offset plus computed delta
Not setting APPEND_ONLY=FALSE when updates/deletes need to be captured, not just new inserts
Querying the stream in a plain SELECT and assuming that alone advances the offset
Decoupling the stream consumption and the DML into separate transactions, risking lost or duplicated changes
Not checking SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA, wasting warehouse credits on empty scheduled runs
keyPoints: A stream stores an offset into the source table's change tracking, not copies of the changed rows
METADATA$ACTION and METADATA$ISUPDATE identify insert/delete/update (update = paired delete+insert)
The offset only advances when a DML statement consumes the stream inside a committing transaction
Coupling stream consumption and DML in one transaction prevents both lost and duplicated changes on failure
A failed/rolled-back task leaves the offset unchanged, so the next run safely reprocesses the same delta
SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA avoids wasting warehouse credits on empty scheduled runs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a stream tracks (offset + computed delta, not stored rows)
Correctly explains METADATA$ACTION/ISUPDATE semantics
Correctly explains offset advancement tied to committing DML in the same transaction
Explains failure/rollback behavior and why it is safe
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Configure Auto Loader for Safe Schema Evolution on a Semi-Structured Source
questions.prompt: Write a PySpark Auto Loader read configuration for a JSON source where upstream producers occasionally add new fields and, less often, change a field's type. Configure it so new fields don't break the stream, but a genuine type change is surfaced for a human decision rather than silently coerced or silently dropped. Explain the mechanics of the schema evolution mode you chose and what actually happens on each kind of change.
questions.modelAnswer:
`cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode = "addNewColumns"` is the setting doing the specific job the prompt asks for: when Auto Loader detects a genuinely new field that isn't in its tracked schema (stored at `cloudFiles.schemaLocation`), it adds that column going forward and -- critically -- fails the current micro-batch once, with a clear UnknownFieldException-style error, rather than silently either dropping the new field or silently inferring and merging it without anyone noticing. The stream is designed to be restarted immediately after that failure; on restart, Auto Loader has already recorded the updated schema (including the new column) and new micro-batches proceed normally with the wider schema, backfilling NULLs for the new column in any already-processed historical rows. So new fields don't permanently break the stream, but they do deliberately interrupt it once, as a signal, rather than passing through invisibly -- which the prompt describes as acceptable ('new fields don't break the stream' means the pipeline recovers automatically on restart, not that it never notices).

A genuine type change on an existing field -- say a field that was always an integer starts arriving as a string -- is a different and more dangerous case, and `addNewColumns` mode does not silently coerce it: Auto Loader's schema inference treats a type mismatch against the already-recorded schema as a parse/read error for the affected records by default (they land in Auto Loader's rescued-data column, `_rescued_data`, if that's enabled, or fail the batch), rather than attempting an implicit cast that could quietly corrupt values (e.g., silently truncating or misparsing a string that happens to look numeric). That's exactly the 'surfaced for a human decision' behavior the prompt wants -- a type change is not treated the same as a new-field addition, because changing a type retroactively affects how every existing row in that column should be interpreted, which is a decision a schema-evolution mode shouldn't make silently on your behalf.

The alternative modes are worth knowing precisely because they'd fail this requirement: `rescue` would route any new or mismatched field into the `_rescued_data` column without ever updating the tracked schema or failing the batch, which hides new fields from downstream consumers entirely; `failOnNewColumns` would halt the stream on any new field, including harmless additive ones, requiring manual intervention for every routine schema addition; and `none` would simply not track schema evolution at all. `addNewColumns` is the one mode that treats additive changes as low-risk-and-self-healing while still surfacing (via a hard batch failure, not silent handling) anything it can't confidently reconcile on its own, including genuine type changes.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The setting that matters most here is schemaEvolutionMode set to addNewColumns, because that's specifically designed to treat 'a new field showed up' as a safe, self-healing event rather than an emergency. When Auto Loader sees a field it's never tracked before, it does fail the current micro-batch once -- that's intentional, it's basically Auto Loader saying 'heads up, I found something new' -- but it also immediately records the updated schema, so when you restart the stream, it just picks up with the wider schema and keeps going, backfilling nulls for the new column on older rows. So in practice, new fields cause one controlled hiccup, not an ongoing break.

A real type change on an existing field is treated completely differently, and deliberately so. Auto Loader isn't going to quietly decide that a field which used to be an integer is now fine to read as a string, or silently cast one into the other, because that's exactly the kind of decision that can corrupt data without anyone noticing -- think of a numeric-looking string getting misparsed. Instead that record either fails to parse or lands in the rescued-data column if you've enabled it, which is the 'surfaced for a human' behavior you want -- someone has to actually look at it and decide how to handle the type change, rather than the pipeline guessing.

I'd also mention why I didn't pick one of the other modes: rescue would quietly stash anything unexpected without ever updating the schema, which means new fields become invisible to everyone downstream instead of becoming real columns; and failOnNewColumns would treat every single new field, even a harmless additive one, as a reason to halt and wait for a human, which is overkill for the common case this pipeline actually needs to self-heal from.
commonMistakes: Using rescue mode and assuming new fields still become real, queryable columns
Assuming addNewColumns silently handles type changes the same way it handles new fields
Not knowing the first batch after a new field appears is expected to fail and that a restart is required
Using failOnNewColumns for a source where additive schema changes are routine and should self-heal
Forgetting to set a schemaLocation, without which Auto Loader cannot track schema across restarts
keyPoints: addNewColumns mode treats new fields as additive and self-healing after one controlled batch failure + restart
The failure on a new field is intentional, signaling the schema changed, not a bug to suppress
Type changes on existing fields are not silently coerced; affected records fail or are rescued, not merged
schemaLocation persists the tracked schema across stream restarts
Alternative modes (rescue, failOnNewColumns, none) each fail this requirement in a different way
This design deliberately distinguishes additive changes (safe) from type changes (require human judgment)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly configures addNewColumns schema evolution mode
Correctly explains the restart-required mechanics for new fields
Correctly explains that type changes are not silently coerced
Correctly contrasts against alternative schema evolution modes
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Write a Fabric Eventstream-to-KQL Query for Real-Time Fraud Signal Detection
questions.prompt: Write a KQL query against a Fabric Eventhouse table (fed by an Eventstream from a payments topic) that flags a session as a potential fraud signal when the same card_id attempts more than 5 transactions within a 2-minute sliding window. Explain why this kind of windowed aggregation belongs in the real-time (KQL/Eventstream) layer rather than waiting for the next batch/lakehouse run.
questions.code:
PaymentEvents
| where ingestion_time() > ago(10m)
| summarize txn_count = count(), amounts = make_list(amount)
    by card_id, bin = bin(EventTimestamp, 2m)
| where txn_count > 5
| extend risk_flag = "velocity_breach",
         detected_at = now()
| project card_id, bin, txn_count, amounts, risk_flag, detected_at

// For a true sliding (not fixed-bucket) window, use series_decompose or
// a rolling count via arg_max over a materialized view with hopping windows:
.create-or-alter materialized-view CardVelocity on table PaymentEvents
{
    PaymentEvents
    | summarize txn_count = count() by card_id, bin(EventTimestamp, 30s)
}
questions.modelAnswer:
The first query uses `bin(EventTimestamp, 2m)` to group transactions into fixed, non-overlapping 2-minute buckets, which is a reasonable first pass but has a known edge case: a card making 3 transactions in the last 10 seconds of one bucket and 3 more in the first 10 seconds of the next bucket produces 6 transactions in 20 seconds, but no single fixed bucket shows more than 3, so the fixed-bin approach can miss velocity bursts that straddle a bucket boundary. A true sliding window needs either a smaller bucket size with an explicit rolling sum across adjacent buckets, or a hopping-window materialized view (narrower bins like 30 seconds, summed over the trailing N bins at query time) to approximate a continuously sliding 2-minute check without the boundary blind spot -- the tradeoff is real-time query cost/complexity versus detection precision, and for a fraud signal specifically, the boundary blind spot is a real risk worth paying for finer bins to close.

This class of detection belongs in the real-time layer specifically because the value of a fraud signal decays to near zero with latency: the entire point of catching 'more than 5 transactions on this card in 2 minutes' is to act on it -- block the card, trigger a step-up authentication, alert a fraud analyst -- while the fraud attempt is still in progress, not after a batch job runs at the next scheduled interval, which could be minutes to hours later and well after the fraudulent transactions have already settled. KQL over an Eventhouse fed by an Eventstream is built for exactly this: sub-second-to-low-second ingestion-to-query latency on streaming data, versus a lakehouse/batch pipeline that's optimized for throughput and historical analysis, not for being queried continuously within seconds of an event landing.

That said, the real-time layer isn't a replacement for the batch layer here -- it's a complement. The real-time KQL query is tuned to catch an obvious, high-confidence velocity signal fast and cheaply; genuinely sophisticated fraud-model scoring (features built from weeks of a cardholder's history, cross-referencing device fingerprints, ML-model inference) still belongs in the batch/lakehouse layer, feeding back into a blocklist or risk score that the real-time layer can then check against on every new transaction. The real-time query's job is narrow and fast; the batch layer's job is deep and comprehensive, and a production fraud system needs both operating together, not one replacing the other.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd ship the first version of this query, but I'd flag its real limitation right away: bin() creates fixed, non-overlapping buckets, so a burst that straddles the boundary between two buckets -- say three fast transactions right at the end of one 2-minute window and three more right at the start of the next -- never shows up as 'more than 5 in 2 minutes' in any single bucket, even though it genuinely was. For a first pass that's often good enough to catch the obvious cases, but if this is actually going into a fraud pipeline, I'd move to a hopping-window materialized view with much smaller bins -- 30 seconds, say -- and sum over the trailing several bins at query time, so the detection isn't blind to anything that happens to land on a boundary.

As for why this needs to live in the real-time layer at all rather than waiting for the next lakehouse batch run: the entire value of a fraud signal is in acting on it before the damage is done. If I detect 'five rapid transactions on this card' an hour from now in a batch job, the fraudulent charges have probably already gone through and settled -- the signal arrived too late to be useful for the thing it's actually for, which is blocking the card or triggering extra verification while the attempt is still happening. KQL over an Eventhouse is built specifically for that kind of low-latency, continuously-updating query over a streaming table; a lakehouse pipeline is optimized for throughput over historical data, not for being hit with the same query every few seconds.

I'd also be clear that this isn't meant to replace deeper fraud modeling -- the real-time query here is a fast, cheap tripwire for an obvious pattern. The heavier ML-based fraud scoring, built on weeks of behavioral history, still belongs in the batch layer, and ideally feeds a blocklist or risk score back that this real-time query can check against too.
commonMistakes: Assuming bin()-based fixed windows are equivalent to a true sliding window
Not recognizing the boundary blind spot where a burst straddling two buckets goes undetected
Treating real-time detection as a replacement for, rather than a complement to, deeper batch fraud modeling
Underestimating how much value a fraud signal loses with even minutes of latency
Not considering hopping-window materialized views as a way to approximate true sliding-window detection
keyPoints: bin()-based fixed windows can miss bursts that straddle a bucket boundary
A true sliding/hopping window needs smaller bins summed across a trailing range
Fraud signal value decays rapidly with latency, making real-time detection necessary, not optional
KQL over an Eventhouse/Eventstream is built for sub-second-to-low-second query latency on streaming data
Real-time detection complements, not replaces, deeper batch-layer fraud modeling
A production fraud system typically needs both a fast real-time tripwire and a deep batch model

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a plausible KQL windowed-aggregation query
Correctly identifies the fixed-bucket boundary limitation and a fix
Correctly argues why this belongs in the real-time layer (latency decay of signal value)
Correctly frames real-time detection as complementary to batch fraud modeling
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Write a Retry-Safe Snapshot Isolation Handler for a 3960 Update Conflict
questions.prompt: Write T-SQL (or a thin wrapper procedure) that catches error 3960 ('Snapshot isolation transaction aborted due to update conflict') under SNAPSHOT isolation and retries the transaction correctly -- meaning it re-reads the data it needs, not just blindly re-executes the original write. Explain why a naive retry loop that just resubmits the same UPDATE statement is not actually safe.
questions.modelAnswer:
A 3960 error means the transaction's snapshot -- the data as it looked at the moment the transaction began -- is now stale with respect to a row the transaction tried to write, because some other transaction committed a change to that exact row after this transaction's snapshot was taken. SQL Server aborts the writer in that situation rather than silently letting it overwrite a change it never actually saw, which is the whole point of snapshot isolation's write-write conflict detection: it protects against a lost-update anomaly, where blindly overwriting based on stale data would silently discard someone else's committed change.

A naive retry that just re-executes the exact same UPDATE statement with the exact same computed value is unsafe for exactly that reason: if the original statement computed its new value from data read earlier in the same aborted transaction (e.g., `SET Quantity = @OldQuantityReadEarlier + @Delta`), resubmitting it verbatim reapplies a delta computed against data that's now known to be stale -- it doesn't pick up whatever the conflicting transaction actually changed, so the retry can still produce a logically wrong result even though it 'succeeds' the second time, just without colliding with that exact transaction again.

The correct retry pattern, shown in the stored procedure, starts a brand-new transaction on each attempt and re-reads `@CurrentQty` fresh inside that new transaction before recomputing the update -- so attempt 2 is computing its new value from the actual current state of the row, including whatever the conflicting transaction just committed, not from a value captured before the conflict was even detected. The CATCH block specifically checks `ERROR_NUMBER() = 3960` before deciding to retry -- any other error is re-thrown immediately rather than retried, because blindly retrying on every exception would mask real bugs (a constraint violation, a genuine business-rule failure) as if they were transient conflicts. Bounding the retry count and adding a small backoff (`WAITFOR DELAY`) prevents a pathological hot-row scenario from spinning indefinitely under sustained contention.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The thing I'd explain first is what a 3960 actually means: it's not a generic error, it's SQL Server specifically telling you 'the row you just tried to write has changed since your transaction's snapshot was taken, and I'm not going to let you silently overwrite that change.' That's a deliberate safety mechanism against a lost update, not a bug to work around with a dumb retry.

And that's exactly why a naive retry that just resubmits the same UPDATE is dangerous -- if that UPDATE's new value was computed from data read earlier, before the conflict happened, resubmitting it verbatim ignores whatever the other transaction actually changed. It might succeed the second time because it no longer collides with that specific transaction, but the value it writes is still based on stale information -- you've silently produced a wrong result while looking like you recovered gracefully.

The fix is to make the retry re-read everything it needs fresh, inside a brand-new transaction, every single attempt -- which is exactly what this procedure does: on a 3960, it loops back, starts a new transaction, and re-selects the current quantity before recomputing anything. I'd also point out the CATCH block only retries on error 3960 specifically -- anything else gets re-thrown immediately, because if I caught every error and retried blindly, I'd be masking real bugs, like a genuine constraint violation, as if they were just transient contention. And I bound the attempts with a small delay between them, because under real hot-row contention you don't want this spinning forever -- at some point it should fail loudly instead of quietly looping.
commonMistakes: Treating 3960 as a generic transient error to retry blindly, like a deadlock, without understanding its cause
Retrying by resubmitting the exact same UPDATE without re-reading the underlying data fresh
Catching and retrying on every error type instead of specifically checking for 3960
Not bounding the retry count, risking indefinite spinning under sustained hot-row contention
Not rolling back the aborted transaction explicitly before starting a new attempt
keyPoints: 3960 signals a write-write conflict: the row changed since the transaction's snapshot was taken
This is deliberate lost-update protection, not a bug
Resubmitting the same UPDATE verbatim can apply a delta computed from now-stale data
A correct retry starts a new transaction and re-reads the current data fresh before recomputing
Only ERROR_NUMBER() = 3960 should trigger a retry; other errors should propagate immediately
Retry attempts should be bounded with backoff to avoid indefinite spinning under contention

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what error 3960 signals and why it occurs
Correctly explains why a naive resubmit-retry is unsafe
Implements a correct retry pattern that re-reads data fresh on each attempt
Correctly scopes retry logic to error 3960 only, with bounded attempts
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Write a GitHub Actions Workflow That Gates a dbt Monorepo Build on Changed Projects Only
questions.prompt: Write a GitHub Actions workflow for a monorepo containing multiple dbt projects (one per business domain) where a PR should only trigger CI (Slim CI build + tests) for the dbt project(s) whose files actually changed, not the entire monorepo. Explain the tradeoff this path-filtering approach makes versus simply running CI for every project on every PR, and what risk it introduces that the team needs to mitigate.
questions.code:
name: dbt-slim-ci
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - 'dbt_projects/**'

jobs:
  detect-changes:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      projects: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.changes }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dorny/paths-filter@v3
        id: filter
        with:
          filters: |
            finance: 'dbt_projects/finance/**'
            marketing: 'dbt_projects/marketing/**'
            platform: 'dbt_projects/platform/**'

  slim-ci-build:
    needs: detect-changes
    if: needs.detect-changes.outputs.projects != '[]'
    strategy:
      matrix:
        project: ${{ fromJson(needs.detect-changes.outputs.projects) }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install dbt
        run: pip install dbt-snowflake
      - name: Fetch production manifest for ${{ matrix.project }}
        run: |
          aws s3 cp s3://dbt-artifacts/${{ matrix.project }}/manifest.json \
            dbt_projects/${{ matrix.project }}/manifest.json
      - name: Slim CI build
        working-directory: dbt_projects/${{ matrix.project }}
        run: |
          dbt deps
          dbt build --select state:modified+ \
            --state ./manifest.json --defer
questions.modelAnswer:
The `paths-filter` step produces a JSON list of exactly which project directories had files change in this PR's diff, and the matrix job then only spins up a Slim CI build for projects actually in that list -- a PR that only touches `dbt_projects/finance/` never triggers CI for `marketing` or `platform` at all, as opposed to a naive workflow that runs every project's full CI on every PR regardless of what changed. The tradeoff is pure CI-minutes and wall-clock-time savings versus running everything: for a monorepo with several independent dbt projects, most PRs only touch one, so unconditionally running all of them wastes compute and, more importantly, slows down the feedback loop for every contributor waiting on CI to pass before merging.

The risk this introduces is a false sense of safety around cross-project dependencies: if `platform`'s models are referenced across project boundaries by `finance` or `marketing` (via a cross-project `ref()`, a shared macro package, or just an implicit assumption about a shared table's schema), a PR that only touches `platform` and triggers only `platform`'s CI could break `finance` or `marketing` silently, because their CI never ran and had no chance to catch the break -- path-based filtering assumes project boundaries are also dependency boundaries, which isn't automatically true in a monorepo unless the team has deliberately kept it that way.

Mitigating that risk requires either enforcing that cross-project references are genuinely rare/disallowed (keeping each dbt project's CI scope actually isolated, which is the assumption path-filtering depends on), or, if cross-project `ref()`s are a real, supported pattern (dbt Mesh-style), extending the change-detection step to also trigger CI for any downstream project that references a changed project -- essentially doing a project-level dependency graph traversal analogous to what `state:modified+` already does at the model level within a single project, just one layer up. Without that extension, path-filtering silently trusts that project boundaries equal blast-radius boundaries, which is exactly the assumption that eventually gets violated as a monorepo grows and teams start reaching across project lines.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The win here is pretty straightforward -- most PRs in a monorepo like this only touch one project, so there's no reason to spin up CI for marketing and platform when someone only changed a finance model. The paths-filter step figures out which project directories actually changed in the diff, and the matrix job only builds CI for those -- so you get faster feedback and lower CI cost for the common case.

The risk I'd flag immediately, though, is what happens when projects aren't actually as independent as their folder structure suggests. If finance's models reference something in platform -- a shared ref(), a shared macro, even just an assumption about a table's shape -- and a PR only touches platform, this workflow only runs platform's CI. If that platform change breaks something finance depends on, nobody finds out until finance's own CI runs on some unrelated future PR, or worse, in production. Path-based filtering is implicitly betting that project folder boundaries are also dependency boundaries, and that's a bet you have to actively keep true, not something that's automatically guaranteed by organizing the repo this way.

So the mitigation is either a hard rule that cross-project references just aren't allowed -- which keeps this assumption valid by policy -- or, if the team actually wants cross-project refs as a supported pattern, extending the change-detection step to also trigger CI for any project that depends on whatever changed, basically doing the same kind of dependency-aware selection dbt already does with state:modified+, just one level up at the project graph instead of the model graph.
commonMistakes: Assuming project folder boundaries automatically equal dependency/blast-radius boundaries
Not fetching a per-project production manifest, breaking Slim CI's deferral for the filtered project
Running full CI for every project on every PR, wasting compute and slowing feedback for the common case
Not having a policy (or tooling) to detect cross-project references that would invalidate the path-filter assumption
Triggering CI only on direct file changes without considering a project-level dependency graph
keyPoints: paths-filter restricts CI to only the project(s) whose files changed in the PR diff
This trades full-coverage safety for CI speed and cost savings on the common single-project-change case
The hidden risk is cross-project dependencies: an unrelated project's CI never runs even if it depends on the changed code
Path-based filtering assumes project folders are also dependency/blast-radius boundaries
Mitigation: disallow cross-project refs by policy, or extend change-detection to a project-level dependency graph
Each matrix job still needs its own project-scoped production manifest for Slim CI deferral to work

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the path-filtering mechanism and CI-time tradeoff
Correctly identifies the cross-project dependency risk this introduces
Proposes a sound mitigation (policy or dependency-graph-aware triggering)
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Rewrite a T-SQL Recursive CTE for a Target Dialect's Recursion Limits
questions.prompt: Given a T-SQL recursive CTE that walks an employee-manager hierarchy up to 50 levels deep, rewrite it to run correctly on a target platform (e.g., Snowflake or Postgres-family) whose default recursion behavior or limits differ from SQL Server's. Explain specifically what could silently break in a naive copy-paste port, and how your rewrite avoids it.
questions.code:
-- Original T-SQL (default MAXRECURSION = 100, override if hierarchy can exceed it)
WITH EmpHierarchy AS (
  SELECT EmployeeId, ManagerId, Name, 0 AS Level
  FROM dbo.Employees WHERE ManagerId IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.EmployeeId, e.ManagerId, e.Name, h.Level + 1
  FROM dbo.Employees e
  JOIN EmpHierarchy h ON e.ManagerId = h.EmployeeId
)
SELECT * FROM EmpHierarchy OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100);

-- Rewritten for Snowflake: explicit recursion depth guard in the anchor/recursive
-- predicate (Snowflake does not have an OPTION(MAXRECURSION) equivalent and
-- defaults differ), plus an explicit cycle guard against bad data creating
-- an actual infinite loop rather than just a deep-but-finite hierarchy.
WITH RECURSIVE EmpHierarchy AS (
  SELECT EmployeeId, ManagerId, Name, 0 AS Level,
         ARRAY_CONSTRUCT(EmployeeId) AS VisitedPath
  FROM Employees WHERE ManagerId IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.EmployeeId, e.ManagerId, e.Name, h.Level + 1,
         ARRAY_APPEND(h.VisitedPath, e.EmployeeId)
  FROM Employees e
  JOIN EmpHierarchy h ON e.ManagerId = h.EmployeeId
  WHERE h.Level < 100                                   -- explicit depth guard
    AND NOT ARRAY_CONTAINS(e.EmployeeId::VARIANT, h.VisitedPath)  -- explicit cycle guard
)
SELECT * FROM EmpHierarchy;
questions.modelAnswer:
Two things in the original T-SQL are doing load-bearing work that a naive copy-paste port silently drops. First, `OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100)` is an explicit, T-SQL-specific recursion-depth safety valve -- SQL Server's genuine default is 100 anyway, but the clause makes the limit explicit and overridable; a direct syntax port to a target platform simply drops this clause silently because it isn't valid syntax there, and the target platform's own default recursion limit (which varies by platform and is sometimes effectively unlimited, sometimes a different fixed number) now governs behavior instead, with no equivalent warning if the team assumed '100' was still in effect. Second, and more dangerous: SQL Server's recursive CTE engine has some built-in protections against certain cycle patterns, but relying on platform-default cycle handling across a port is risky, because what counts as a 'cycle' and how aggressively the engine detects one before erroring or looping is genuinely platform-specific behavior, not guaranteed-identical SQL semantics -- a hierarchy that's supposed to be acyclic but has bad data (a manager cycle introduced by a data-entry error) could behave completely differently on the target platform: an infinite loop that eventually errors out on a resource limit instead of a cycle-specific error, or worse, silently returning incomplete results depending on how the engine's recursion evaluation order interacts with the bad data.

The rewrite handles both risks explicitly rather than relying on platform defaults. The depth guard (`WHERE h.Level < 100`) is written directly into the recursive member's predicate, reproducing the original's intended depth ceiling without depending on syntax that doesn't exist on the target platform -- it travels with the query itself rather than depending on a session or platform-level default that could silently differ. The cycle guard (`ARRAY_CONTAINS` against an accumulated `VisitedPath`) is new logic that didn't exist in the original at all, added specifically because the original was implicitly relying on SQL Server's own cycle-handling behavior (or just lucky, cycle-free data) rather than defending against bad data explicitly -- on the target platform, that implicit protection can't be assumed to exist in the same form, so the rewrite makes the acyclic assumption an explicit, enforced guarantee instead of an assumption inherited from the source platform's specific engine behavior.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The thing that would bite someone doing a pure copy-paste here is MAXRECURSION. That OPTION clause is SQL Server-specific syntax -- it just doesn't exist on Snowflake or Postgres-family platforms, so a naive port either errors out immediately on invalid syntax, or if someone strips it out to make it parse, the query now silently runs under whatever that target platform's own default recursion limit happens to be, which isn't guaranteed to match SQL Server's 100. If the hierarchy actually needs closer to that limit, you could get a different failure -- or a different silent truncation -- on the new platform with zero indication anything changed.

The second thing, which is honestly scarier because it's less obvious, is cycle protection. If this hierarchy's data ever has a bad row -- someone got assigned as their own manager's manager two levels up by mistake -- SQL Server's recursive CTE engine has its own specific way of dealing with that, and I wouldn't assume the target platform handles it identically. You could go from a clean error on one platform to an actual runaway, resource-exhausting loop on the other, or to silently wrong results, depending on engine internals that were never guaranteed to be the same across platforms in the first place.

So in the rewrite, I didn't just translate syntax -- I made both of those things explicit instead of implicit. The depth check is now a literal WHERE clause inside the recursive member, so it travels with the query and doesn't depend on any platform-specific option syntax existing at all. And I added an explicit visited-path cycle check using an array, which wasn't in the original, specifically because I don't want to rely on 'the engine will probably catch a cycle somehow' -- I want the query itself to refuse to revisit a node it's already seen, regardless of which platform it's running on.
commonMistakes: Assuming MAXRECURSION-equivalent syntax exists on every target platform
Dropping the recursion-depth safety valve entirely rather than reimplementing it explicitly
Assuming cycle-detection behavior is identical across platforms rather than engine-specific
Not adding an explicit cycle guard when porting a hierarchy query that relied on source-platform cycle handling
Treating a copy-paste of recursive CTE syntax as sufficient without testing against intentionally bad/cyclic data
keyPoints: OPTION (MAXRECURSION) is T-SQL-specific syntax with no direct equivalent on most other platforms
Dropping it silently hands control to the target platform's own, potentially different, default recursion limit
Cycle-handling behavior for bad/cyclic data is engine-specific, not guaranteed-identical SQL semantics
A safe rewrite makes the depth limit an explicit predicate inside the recursive member
A safe rewrite adds an explicit cycle guard (e.g., visited-path tracking) rather than relying on platform defaults
Both guards should be tested against intentionally bad/cyclic data before trusting the port

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies MAXRECURSION as non-portable T-SQL-specific syntax
Correctly identifies cycle-handling as a platform-specific risk, not guaranteed-identical behavior
Rewrite correctly implements an explicit depth guard
Rewrite correctly implements an explicit cycle guard
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Diagnosing Recurring Deadlocks That Only Appear During the Nightly Batch Window
questions.prompt: Deadlock graphs (from a deadlock monitor extended event session) show the same two stored procedures colliding every night, but only during the batch window -- never during the day under lighter load. The procedures haven't changed in months. Walk through how you'd actually diagnose the root cause using the deadlock graph's lock/resource information, and what's most likely different at night that's triggering a long-dormant lock-ordering issue.
questions.modelAnswer:
The deadlock graph's XML gives you the exact resource each session was holding and waiting on at the moment of the collision -- the specific lock type (key, page, RID), the object and index involved, and each session's last-executed statement. The first thing I'd check is whether the two procedures are genuinely always acquiring locks on the same two resources in opposite order (a true lock-order inversion) or whether it's a newer pattern: lock escalation. SQL Server escalates row/page locks to a table-level lock automatically once a single statement accumulates roughly 5,000 locks (or crosses certain memory thresholds), and that escalation threshold is far more likely to be crossed during the nightly batch window specifically because batch volume is much higher at night -- the exact same procedure that takes out a handful of row locks during the day, staying well under the escalation threshold and never actually colliding with the other procedure's rows, can escalate to a table lock at night under batch-sized row counts, and a table lock collides with far more of what the other procedure touches than the handful of specific rows it would have locked during the day.

That's the most likely explanation for 'the procedures haven't changed but the deadlock only shows up at night': the code is unchanged, but the data volume per execution has not been, and lock escalation is a volume-triggered behavior, not a code-triggered one -- it can turn two procedures that genuinely never conflict at low row counts into two procedures that reliably conflict once nightly batch sizes push either one over the escalation threshold.

To confirm it, I'd pull `sys.dm_tran_locks` or re-examine the deadlock graph specifically for an escalated lock mode (an `OBJECT`-level lock rather than `KEY`/`PAGE`) on one or both sessions at the time of the deadlock, and compare typical nightly batch row counts for each procedure's affected statement against the ~5,000-lock escalation threshold. If that's confirmed, the fix is to reduce the row count any single statement touches per transaction during the batch window specifically -- chunking the nightly batch into smaller transactions so no single statement crosses the escalation threshold -- rather than assuming the code itself has a latent bug that somehow only manifests at night.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The detail that jumps out immediately is 'the procedures haven't changed, but it only happens at night' -- that phrase almost always points to something volume-triggered rather than a logic bug, and the first thing I'd suspect is lock escalation. SQL Server will automatically bump row or page locks up to a full table lock once a single statement crosses roughly 5,000 locks. During the day, with lighter load, these two procedures might each only ever touch a handful of rows and never actually collide. At night, the same code processing a much bigger batch can quietly cross that escalation threshold and grab a table-level lock instead -- and a table lock collides with way more of what the other procedure is doing than a few specific row locks ever would.

To confirm that instead of guessing, I'd go back into the deadlock graph XML and look specifically at the lock mode each session was holding -- if I see an object-level lock instead of key or page-level locks at the time of the deadlock, that's the escalation signature right there. I'd pair that with pulling the actual row counts each procedure processed during a recent nightly run versus a daytime run, to confirm the volume difference is enough to plausibly cross that ~5,000-lock threshold.

If that's confirmed, I wouldn't go hunting for a code bug that isn't there -- the fix is to chunk the nightly batch into smaller transactions, so no single statement's lock count gets anywhere near the escalation threshold, which keeps both procedures operating with row/page-level locks the way they do safely during the day.
commonMistakes: Assuming unchanged code rules out a volume-triggered cause like lock escalation
Not checking the deadlock graph for escalated (object-level) lock modes versus row/page-level locks
Treating a time-of-day-only deadlock as inherently a scheduling/concurrency coincidence rather than investigating volume
Jumping straight to adding indexes or NOLOCK hints without confirming the actual lock mode involved
Not comparing actual row counts processed per statement between daytime and nighttime runs
keyPoints: Deadlock graph XML reveals exact lock type/resource and each session's last statement
Lock escalation (row/page to table lock) triggers automatically around ~5,000 locks per statement
Nightly batch volume is the likely trigger for escalation that doesn't occur during lighter daytime load
An escalated table lock collides with far more than the specific rows involved, explaining the new conflict
Confirm via sys.dm_tran_locks or the deadlock graph's lock mode (OBJECT vs KEY/PAGE)
Fix is chunking the nightly batch into smaller transactions, not rewriting unchanged business logic

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies lock escalation as the likely volume-triggered cause
Correctly explains the ~5,000-lock escalation threshold and its effect
Proposes a concrete diagnostic method using the deadlock graph/DMVs
Proposes a sound fix (batch chunking) over an unnecessary code rewrite

questions.title: A dbt Mart Is 'Correct' But Produces Three Different Revenue Numbers in Three BI Tools
questions.prompt: Finance, Sales, and Marketing each pull 'total revenue' from the same dbt-built fct_revenue mart through three different BI tools, and get three different numbers for the same month, even though every individual row in the mart is verifiably correct. Walk through the most likely structural cause of this -- and why re-checking the SQL logic in the model itself usually won't find it -- and explain the fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
When every row in the underlying mart is individually correct but aggregating 'the same metric' produces different totals depending on which tool computes it, the almost-certain cause is join fanout happening somewhere between the mart and the point of aggregation -- not a bug in fct_revenue's own SQL. Fanout happens when a fact table (or a mart built from one) is joined to a dimension that has a one-to-many, not one-to-one, relationship with the fact grain: joining fct_revenue (one row per order line, say) to a dim_customer_snapshot that has multiple rows per customer over time (an SCD Type 2 table) without an effective-dating predicate correctly scoping exactly one snapshot row per fact row will multiply some fact rows across multiple matching dimension rows, inflating the sum of revenue for any customer whose dimension history has more than one row overlapping the join condition.

The reason re-checking fct_revenue's own SQL doesn't find it is that the fanout isn't happening inside the model that was checked -- fct_revenue itself, considered row by row, is correct; the multiplication happens downstream, at whatever layer actually performs the join and aggregation that each BI tool is independently constructing. If Finance's tool joins fct_revenue to a customer dimension one way, Sales' tool joins it slightly differently (maybe filtering to only 'current' dimension rows, maybe not), and Marketing's semantic layer or report builder does a third thing, each tool can be computing a structurally different join against the same underlying fact table, and getting a different -- sometimes inflated, sometimes correctly non-inflated -- total as a direct consequence, with no single model's SQL being 'wrong' in isolation.

The durable fix is not to inspect each BI tool's query one at a time and patch its join logic -- that just relocates the problem to the next tool that gets added -- but to define 'total revenue' exactly once, in a governed layer that every tool is required to go through: a dbt Semantic Layer / MetricFlow metric definition (or an equivalent BI-tool-agnostic semantic layer) that encodes the correct join and aggregation logic centrally, so Finance, Sales, and Marketing's tools all query the same metric definition rather than each independently re-deriving 'revenue' from the raw mart with their own join assumptions. That turns 'three tools, three join implementations, three numbers' into 'three tools, one metric definition, one number' -- the fix is architectural (centralizing the metric logic) rather than a SQL patch to any one of the three tools' individual queries.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The fact that every row checks out individually but the totals still disagree is actually the biggest clue here -- it tells me the bug isn't in fct_revenue's SQL at all, it's happening downstream, at whatever point each tool joins and aggregates the mart. The classic cause is join fanout: if somewhere between the mart and the final number, revenue gets joined to a dimension that has more than one row per key -- a customer snapshot table with history, say -- and that join doesn't correctly scope to exactly one matching row, some revenue rows get counted more than once. Finance's tool might join it one way, Sales' tool a slightly different way, Marketing's a third way, and each one can produce a different total from the exact same underlying fact rows, with none of them technically having 'wrong' SQL in isolation.

That's exactly why re-reading fct_revenue's model code won't find it -- you're looking in the one place that's actually correct. The problem lives in three separate, independently-built join-and-aggregate layers that nobody centrally controls.

So I wouldn't go fix each BI tool's query one at a time -- that just means the next tool someone adds repeats the same mistake. I'd push to define revenue exactly once, in something like dbt's Semantic Layer with a MetricFlow metric definition, so the correct join and aggregation logic lives in one governed place, and every tool -- Finance's, Sales', Marketing's -- queries that single metric definition instead of each re-deriving its own join against the raw mart. Once that's in place, there's only one place revenue can be computed wrong, and it's the one place everyone's actually looking at.
commonMistakes: Re-auditing the mart's own SQL when the individual rows are already confirmed correct
Fixing each BI tool's query independently instead of centralizing the metric definition
Not recognizing join fanout from an SCD/snapshot dimension without effective-dating as the likely cause
Assuming three different totals means three different bugs rather than one structural pattern
Not considering a semantic layer (dbt Semantic Layer/MetricFlow) as the architectural fix
keyPoints: Correct individual rows plus inconsistent aggregated totals points to fanout downstream of the mart, not within it
Fanout occurs when a join to a non-unique-per-key dimension (e.g., an un-effective-dated SCD snapshot) multiplies fact rows
