Each BI tool may independently construct a different join, producing different totals from the same correct mart
Re-checking the mart's SQL alone cannot find a bug that occurs downstream in each tool's own query layer
The durable fix centralizes the metric definition (e.g., dbt Semantic Layer/MetricFlow) rather than patching each tool
Centralizing the definition turns multiple independent join implementations into one governed calculation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses join fanout as the likely structural cause
Correctly explains why the mart's own SQL being correct does not rule this out
Correctly identifies that each BI tool may independently reconstruct a different join
Recommends a sound architectural fix (semantic layer/metric centralization)

questions.title: A dbt Snapshot-to-Fact Join Silently Duplicates Rows Without Effective Dating
questions.prompt: A dbt model joins a fact table (one row per transaction) to a dbt snapshot table tracking customer tier changes over time, to tag each transaction with 'customer tier at time of transaction.' The join is on customer_id alone. Row counts in the output are higher than the input fact table's row count. Diagnose exactly why, and write out the corrected join logic.
questions.code:
-- Buggy: joins on customer_id alone against every historical snapshot row
SELECT f.transaction_id, f.transaction_date, f.amount, s.tier
FROM fct_transactions f
JOIN snapshot_customer_tier s ON f.customer_id = s.customer_id;

-- Fixed: effective-dated join scoping to exactly one snapshot row per transaction
SELECT f.transaction_id, f.transaction_date, f.amount, s.tier
FROM fct_transactions f
JOIN snapshot_customer_tier s
  ON f.customer_id = s.customer_id
  AND f.transaction_date >= s.dbt_valid_from
  AND (f.transaction_date < s.dbt_valid_to OR s.dbt_valid_to IS NULL);
questions.modelAnswer:
A dbt snapshot table keeps one row per distinct historical state of each tracked key, with dbt_valid_from and dbt_valid_to (or dbt_updated_at, depending on snapshot strategy) marking the time range each row was the 'current' value -- so a customer who's changed tiers three times over their history has three rows in the snapshot table, all sharing the same customer_id. Joining `ON f.customer_id = s.customer_id` alone, with no condition narrowing to exactly one of those rows, matches every transaction for that customer against all three of that customer's historical tier rows simultaneously -- a single transaction row fans out into three output rows, one per tier-history row, which is exactly why the output row count exceeds the input fact table's row count. The row-level data itself isn't wrong per se (each output row correctly pairs a real transaction with a real historical tier value that customer held at some point), but the join as written has no way of knowing which of those tier values was actually true at the specific moment of that specific transaction, so it returns all of them.

The fix is an effective-dated join: adding `f.transaction_date >= s.dbt_valid_from AND (f.transaction_date < s.dbt_valid_to OR s.dbt_valid_to IS NULL)` as additional join predicates scopes the match to exactly the one snapshot row whose valid-time range actually contains the transaction's timestamp -- the still-current row has a NULL dbt_valid_to, which the OR clause has to handle explicitly, or every transaction against a customer's current, still-open tier period would be silently dropped instead of matched. With that range condition in place, each transaction matches exactly one historical tier row (assuming the snapshot's valid-time ranges are genuinely non-overlapping, which they should be by construction for a well-formed Type-2 snapshot), and the output row count equals the input fact table's row count again.

This is the same underlying fanout pattern as joining to any multi-row-per-key dimension without effective dating -- the fix generalizes to any fact-to-snapshot join: always add the valid-time range predicate, and always explicitly handle the NULL/open-ended dbt_valid_to case for whichever row is currently active.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The row count going up immediately tells me this is a fanout bug, and the join condition confirms exactly why: it's only matching on customer_id, with nothing narrowing it down to a specific point in time. A dbt snapshot table keeps one row per historical version of that customer's tier, so if someone's changed tiers three times, they've got three rows in that snapshot table, all sharing the same customer_id. Joining on customer_id alone matches every one of that customer's transactions against all three of those historical rows at once -- a single transaction fans out into three output rows, which is exactly the inflation being seen.

The fix is to add an effective-dating condition to the join -- essentially 'only match the snapshot row whose valid-from/valid-to range actually covers this transaction's date.' That's the part that was missing entirely; the join was asking 'who is this customer' but never asking 'and which version of their history was true right then.'

The one gotcha I'd flag in the fix itself: the currently-active snapshot row typically has a NULL dbt_valid_to, since it hasn't been superseded yet, so the condition needs to explicitly handle that NULL case with an OR, otherwise every transaction against a customer's current, still-open tier period would get silently dropped from the join instead of correctly matched -- which would quietly swap one bug (too many rows) for another (missing rows) if you're not careful.
commonMistakes: Joining a fact table to a Type-2 snapshot on the natural key alone, without a valid-time range condition
Not understanding that a snapshot table legitimately holds multiple rows per key by design
Fixing the range condition but forgetting to handle the NULL dbt_valid_to case for the currently-active row
Assuming higher output row count than input row count is a data-quality issue rather than a join-logic issue
Not verifying snapshot valid-time ranges are genuinely non-overlapping before relying on exactly-one-match logic
keyPoints: A dbt snapshot holds one row per historical state of a key, with dbt_valid_from/dbt_valid_to marking validity ranges
Joining on the natural key alone matches every historical row, fanning out each fact row
Output row count exceeding input row count is the signature symptom of this kind of fanout
The fix adds an effective-dated range predicate scoping the join to exactly one matching snapshot row
The currently-active row's NULL dbt_valid_to must be explicitly handled or active-period transactions get dropped
This fanout pattern generalizes to any fact-to-history-tracking-dimension join without effective dating

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the cause as a missing effective-date join predicate
Correctly explains why output row count exceeds input row count
Writes a correct effective-dated join fix
Correctly handles the NULL dbt_valid_to case for the active row

questions.title: An Airflow DAG Fails Only in Production With Identical Code
questions.prompt: A DAG runs successfully every time in a local/dev Airflow environment, but fails in production with the same DAG file, the same task code, and the same dbt project checked out at the same commit. Walk through the systematic process for diagnosing this -- what category of difference you'd suspect first and why, and the specific things you'd check, in order.
questions.modelAnswer:
'Identical code, different environment, different outcome' almost always points away from the code itself and toward environment and connection configuration -- things that are, by design, not supposed to live in the code or be checked into version control at all, which is exactly why 'the code is identical' doesn't rule them out as the cause. The first thing I'd check, in order, is Airflow Connections and Variables: production and dev Airflow instances have their own separate metadata databases, so a Connection ID referenced identically in the DAG code (e.g., `snowflake_default`) can point to genuinely different, or differently-configured, credentials, hosts, warehouses, or roles in each environment -- a dev connection might have broader permissions or point at a smaller/more forgiving warehouse than the production connection, so the exact same query can succeed in dev and fail with a permissions or resource error in prod.

Second, I'd check environment variables and installed package versions on the actual worker executing the task -- dev might be running on an engineer's local Airflow with a slightly different Python/provider-package version than the production worker image, even if nobody intended that drift; a provider package version mismatch can change default behavior or introduce/remove a bug between versions silently. Third, I'd check network/firewall reachability specifically from the production worker's network location to whatever the task needs to reach -- a dev environment often runs with far more permissive outbound network access than a locked-down production VPC, so a task that needs to reach an external API or a specific database port can fail purely on network policy in prod while working fine in dev, with the DAG code never seeing or logging a meaningful difference until the connection attempt itself times out or gets refused.

Fourth, and often overlooked, is resource constraints at the infrastructure level -- production workers may have tighter memory/CPU limits or run many more concurrent tasks competing for the same resource pool than a comparatively idle dev instance, so a task that's borderline on memory usage can get OOM-killed in prod specifically because of contention from other tasks that simply don't exist in a single-engineer's dev environment. The systematic order here --connections/variables first, then package/environment versions, then network reachability, then resource contention -- reflects which category is cheapest to check and most likely to be the actual cause for a 'same code, different environment' failure, before ever assuming the DAG logic itself is somehow nondeterministic.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The phrase 'identical code, different result' is actually the whole diagnosis pointing me in the right direction before I even open a log -- if the code's truly the same, the bug has to be in something that was never part of the code to begin with, which almost always means connections, environment config, network, or resources.

So I'd start with Connections and Variables, because those live in each Airflow instance's own metadata database, completely separate from the DAG file. The DAG might reference the exact same connection ID in both places, but that ID can point to a totally different host, warehouse, or set of credentials in prod versus dev -- and a production Snowflake role with tighter permissions, say, can fail on something a wide-open dev role never would have hit.

If that checks out, next I'd look at what's actually installed on the worker running the task -- Python version, provider package versions. It's really common for dev to be running slightly ahead or behind prod without anyone noticing, and a provider package version bump can quietly change default behavior.

After that I'd check network reachability specifically from production's network -- a locked-down prod VPC often blocks outbound traffic that a dev environment never restricted, so a task reaching out to an external API or a specific port can fail purely on firewall rules, with nothing in the DAG code itself showing any sign of trouble until the connection attempt actually times out.

And last, I'd look at resource contention -- is this failing because fifty other tasks are competing for memory on the same production worker pool at that exact time, something a quiet, single-user dev environment would never reproduce. I check these in that order because they're roughly cheapest-to-verify first, and because jumping straight to 'the DAG logic must be nondeterministic' is almost never actually the answer when the code is genuinely unchanged.
commonMistakes: Assuming identical code rules out environment-specific causes and re-reading the DAG logic repeatedly
Not checking that Connections/Variables are independently configured per Airflow metadata database
Overlooking package/provider version drift between dev and production workers
Not considering network/firewall differences between environments as a failure cause
Ignoring resource contention from concurrent production workload as a cause of environment-specific failures
keyPoints: Identical code with different outcomes points to environment/connection/network/resource differences, not logic
Connections and Variables live in each Airflow instance's own metadata database and can differ silently
Package/provider version drift between dev and production workers can change behavior
Production network policy (firewalls/VPC rules) can block reachability that dev never restricted
Production resource contention from concurrent tasks can cause failures a quiet dev environment never reproduces
A systematic, cheapest-first check order avoids wrongly assuming the DAG logic itself is nondeterministic

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons that environment/config, not code, is the likely cause
Correctly identifies Connections/Variables as the first thing to check
Identifies package/version drift as a plausible cause
Identifies network/firewall differences as a plausible cause
Identifies resource contention as a plausible cause

questions.title: Root-Causing a Hot Partition in a High-Throughput Kafka Topic
questions.prompt: A topic partitioned by customer_id has 24 partitions, but consumer lag metrics show lag concentrated almost entirely on 2 of the 24 partitions while the rest sit near zero. Walk through how you'd confirm this is a hot-partition problem, the most likely root cause given a customer_id partition key, and two concrete remediation options with their respective tradeoffs.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first confirmation step is pulling per-partition throughput (messages/sec or bytes/sec written to each partition over a representative window), not just lag -- lag concentrated on 2 of 24 partitions while the rest sit near zero is consistent with either a hot-partition write pattern (a disproportionate volume of messages keyed to land on those 2 partitions) or, less likely given the symmetry, a consumer-side problem specific to those 2 partitions (a stuck consumer thread, an uneven partition assignment within a consumer group). Checking per-partition write throughput first distinguishes these: if those same 2 partitions are also receiving disproportionately more messages written to them, it's a producer-side key-skew problem; if write throughput looks even across all 24 but lag still concentrates on 2, it's more likely a consumer-side issue on whichever consumer instance(s) got assigned those specific partitions.

Given a `customer_id` partition key specifically, the most likely root cause of genuine write-side skew is a small number of disproportionately active keys -- a handful of very large or very active customers (a major enterprise account generating far more events than a typical customer) whose customer_id happens to hash to the same 1-2 partitions, or, in a worse case, a known 'null' or default customer_id value used for some fallback/system-generated events that all land on the same partition because they share the exact same key. Kafka's default partitioner hashes the key to deterministically pick a partition, so any sufficiently skewed key distribution in the real-world data -- not a bug in Kafka itself -- directly produces this exact symptom: a small number of partitions absorbing a disproportionate share of the topic's total write volume because a small number of key values are disproportionately common or disproportionately heavy.

Two concrete remediation options: first, a custom partitioner (or a salted key) that adds a secondary dimension to the partition-selection logic specifically for known high-volume keys -- for example, appending a bucket suffix to the hottest customer_ids' partition key computation to deliberately spread that one customer's events across multiple partitions instead of one -- which fixes the skew but complicates consumption, because now a single customer's events are no longer guaranteed to land on one partition, breaking any downstream logic that depended on partition-level ordering per customer. Second, increasing the partition count for the topic overall, which dilutes the odds of any given key's hash colliding with another hot key's hash onto the same partition, but doesn't fix the problem if a single customer_id is genuinely that disproportionately active on its own (more partitions doesn't un-skew one customer's one key, it only helps when the skew comes from multiple distinct hot keys currently colliding), and repartitioning an existing topic has its own operational cost and potential ordering implications for any consumer relying on existing partition assignments.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Before assuming it's a hot-partition problem, I'd pull per-partition write throughput, not just lag, because the two partitions with all the lag could mean two different things: either those partitions are genuinely getting hammered with more messages than the other 22, or write volume is actually even and something's wrong on the consumer side specifically for whichever consumer got assigned those two partitions. Checking write throughput first tells me which half of the pipeline to actually investigate.

If it is write-side skew, and the partition key is customer_id, the most likely explanation is that a small number of customer_ids are disproportionately active -- maybe one or two huge enterprise accounts generating way more events than a typical customer, or a shared fallback customer_id used for some category of system-generated events that all pile onto the same key, and therefore the same partition, by Kafka's default deterministic hashing. This isn't a Kafka bug, it's just what happens when the real-world key distribution is skewed and you're hashing it to a fixed number of partitions.

For fixing it, one option is a custom or salted partitioner specifically for known hot keys -- basically appending a bucket number to split one customer's events across several partitions instead of one. That solves the skew, but it has a real cost: if anything downstream relies on all of one customer's events landing in order on a single partition, salting breaks that guarantee, and you need to redesign for it.

The other option is just increasing partition count topic-wide, which is simpler to do but doesn't actually help if the problem is one single customer being disproportionately active on their own -- more partitions only helps when multiple distinct hot keys happen to be colliding onto the same partition by chance; it can't un-skew one key that's genuinely that heavy by itself. And repartitioning an existing topic isn't free either -- it has real operational and ordering implications for existing consumers.
commonMistakes: Assuming lag concentration automatically means a hot-partition write problem without checking write throughput first
Not distinguishing a producer-side key-skew problem from a consumer-side assignment/processing problem
Assuming increasing partition count always fixes skew, even when one single key is disproportionately hot
Not recognizing that salting/custom partitioning breaks per-key ordering guarantees downstream consumers may rely on
Treating Kafka's default partitioner behavior as buggy rather than a correct, deterministic response to skewed real-world key distribution
keyPoints: Confirm hot-partition status via per-partition write throughput, not lag alone
Distinguish producer-side key skew from consumer-side assignment/processing issues
A customer_id partition key is especially vulnerable to skew from a small number of very active or shared-default keys
Kafka's deterministic hash-based partitioner correctly reflects real-world key skew; it is not the bug
Custom/salted partitioning fixes skew but breaks per-key ordering guarantees for downstream consumers
Increasing partition count helps only when multiple distinct hot keys collide; it cannot un-skew one disproportionately hot key alone

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes confirming via per-partition write throughput
Correctly identifies likely root cause (skewed key distribution) given customer_id key
Proposes salted/custom partitioning with correct tradeoff (ordering guarantee loss)
Proposes partition count increase with correct limitation (doesn't fix single hot key)
Clear, accurate overall reasoning

questions.title: A Poison-Pill Message Is Silently Stalling an Entire Kafka Consumer Group
questions.prompt: A consumer group's lag is climbing steadily on exactly one partition while every other partition in the same group processes normally. Logs show the same offset being retried repeatedly with no forward progress. Diagnose the likely cause, explain why this specific failure mode can be worse than a consumer simply crashing, and lay out the fix including what must be true about the consumer's commit behavior for the fix to actually work.
questions.modelAnswer:
A single partition's lag climbing steadily while the consumer repeatedly retries the exact same offset is the signature of a poison-pill message: one record at that offset is throwing an exception every time the consumer attempts to process it -- a malformed payload, a schema mismatch, a null field the business logic doesn't handle -- and the consumer's retry loop has no escape hatch, so it keeps reprocessing that same message forever rather than committing past it. Because Kafka consumer offsets are per-partition and strictly sequential (you can't commit offset N+1 while skipping offset N and still correctly represent 'everything up to here has been processed'), the consumer is structurally stuck: it cannot advance past the poison pill without either successfully processing it or deliberately deciding to skip it, and if the code has no deliberate skip logic, it has no way forward at all.

This is genuinely worse than the consumer simply crashing, because a crash is loud and immediately actionable -- an on-call engineer gets paged, the consumer is down, it's obviously broken. A consumer stuck retrying the same poison-pill message can keep running indefinitely, consuming CPU and looking 'alive' in basic health checks, while quietly making zero forward progress on that one partition -- lag climbs steadily and silently, every message behind the poison pill sits unprocessed, and depending on alerting setup, this can go unnoticed far longer than an outright crash would, because 'the consumer process is up and the consumer group shows as active' can mask 'this partition hasn't actually processed anything new in hours.'

The fix is a bounded-retry-then-DLQ (dead letter queue) pattern: attempt to process the message, and after a small, bounded number of retries (to still allow genuinely transient failures to self-resolve), give up on that specific message, route it with failure context to a separate dead-letter topic, and only then commit past its offset. For this to actually work, the consumer's commit behavior has to be structured so the offset commit happens only after the DLQ routing decision is made -- not on a fixed timer via auto-commit, which could either commit past the poison pill prematurely (losing visibility that it ever failed) or, depending on timing, commit before the retry logic even finishes running. Manual, explicit commits tied directly to 'this message has been handled, either successfully or by DLQ routing' are what guarantee the consumer always makes forward progress on the partition while still preserving every failed message for later inspection and reprocessing, instead of either silently skipping failures or getting permanently stuck.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Lag climbing on exactly one partition while the retry logs show the same offset over and over is about as clear a poison-pill signature as you'll see. One specific message -- bad payload, a field the code didn't expect to be null, whatever it is -- is throwing every time the consumer tries to handle it, and because Kafka offsets are strictly sequential per partition, the consumer literally cannot move past that offset without either successfully processing it or deliberately deciding to skip it. If there's no skip logic, it's stuck, full stop.

I'd actually call this worse than a crash, and I'd say that explicitly in an incident writeup if it happened to me, because a crash is loud -- the process is down, it gets noticed and paged immediately. A consumer stuck retrying the same message looks alive. It's consuming CPU, the consumer group shows as active, health checks might even pass, and meanwhile that one partition has made zero real progress for however long this has been going on. That's a much easier failure to miss until someone happens to notice lag climbing.

The fix is giving the consumer an actual escape hatch: retry a bounded number of times to let genuinely transient failures resolve themselves, and if it still fails after that, ship the message to a dead letter topic with context about why it failed, and only then commit past its offset. The thing that has to be true for this to actually work is that the offset commit is tied directly to 'this message has been dealt with, one way or another' -- not on an auto-commit timer. If you're auto-committing on a schedule, you risk either committing past a message that's still being retried, or worse, never actually separating 'successfully processed' from 'gave up and routed to DLQ' in a way the commit logic respects. Manual commit, tied to the actual outcome of processing or DLQ routing, is what keeps the partition moving without quietly losing track of what failed.
commonMistakes: Assuming a stuck-consumer symptom must be a crash or infrastructure issue rather than a specific poison-pill message
Not recognizing that per-partition offsets are strictly sequential, structurally blocking progress without a skip mechanism
Underestimating how a 'silently stuck but alive' consumer is harder to detect than an outright crash
Using auto-commit, which decouples offset advancement from actual processing/DLQ outcome
Retrying indefinitely instead of bounding retries before routing to a dead letter queue
keyPoints: Steady lag growth with the same offset retried repeatedly is the signature of a poison-pill message
Per-partition offsets are strictly sequential, so the consumer cannot skip past a failing message without explicit logic
A stuck-but-running consumer is harder to detect than a crash because it appears healthy on basic checks
Fix: bounded retries, then route to a dead letter topic with failure context, then commit past the offset
Manual commit tied to actual processing/DLQ outcome is required; auto-commit on a timer undermines the fix
The DLQ preserves the failed message for later inspection/reprocessing rather than silently dropping it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses a poison-pill message as the likely cause
Correctly explains sequential offset semantics blocking progress
Correctly explains why this is worse than a crash (silent, appears healthy)
Correctly specifies the bounded-retry-then-DLQ fix and manual commit requirement
Clear, accurate overall reasoning

questions.title: Diagnosing and Fixing Terraform State Drift Discovered Mid-Sprint
questions.prompt: A `terraform plan` on a data platform's infrastructure suddenly shows it wants to destroy and recreate a production storage account that nobody intentionally changed, with no recent merged PRs touching that resource's Terraform code. Walk through how you'd diagnose whether this is genuine drift (someone/something changed the real resource out-of-band) versus a Terraform/provider bug, and the safe remediation process once drift is confirmed -- specifically why you would not just run apply to 'fix' it.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first diagnostic step is `terraform plan` with verbose/detailed output (or `terraform plan -refresh-only` specifically) to see exactly which attribute Terraform believes changed -- a destroy-and-recreate plan (versus an in-place update) specifically means Terraform has detected a change to an attribute that the provider considers immutable/ForceNew for that resource type, so identifying that specific attribute (storage replication type, account tier, a naming/location attribute) tells you precisely what changed, which is the difference between 'someone manually changed the replication setting in the cloud console' and 'the Terraform provider itself updated its schema in a recent version bump and now interprets an unchanged attribute differently.'

To distinguish genuine out-of-band drift from a provider-version artifact, I'd check the cloud provider's own audit/activity log for that specific resource around the time the drift was first noticed -- Azure Activity Log, AWS CloudTrail, or the equivalent -- looking for a write/update event against that storage account from any principal other than the Terraform service identity itself. A genuine out-of-band change (someone manually adjusted a setting in the console, or another automation tool touched the same resource) shows up there with a timestamp and an actor; if nothing shows up in the audit log around the relevant window, I'd next check whether the Terraform provider version was recently bumped (in the lock file or provider block) without a corresponding `terraform plan` being run and reviewed at that time, since a provider update can occasionally change how an existing attribute is read/interpreted even though nothing about the real resource changed at all.

Once drift is confirmed as real (an actual out-of-band change happened), the critical reason not to just run `apply` is that apply, following a destroy-and-recreate plan, will actually destroy the production storage account and its data before recreating it -- which is catastrophic if that account holds live production data, regardless of whether the drift itself was harmless. The safe remediation path is almost never 'let Terraform reconcile it by applying the destructive plan': instead, decide deliberately whether the manual, out-of-band change should become the new desired state (in which case update the Terraform configuration itself to match the new reality, so the next plan shows no diff, without ever running the destructive apply) or whether the manual change was a mistake that needs reverting (in which case revert it directly via the cloud provider's own tooling/console to restore the original setting, again avoiding ever letting Terraform's destroy-and-recreate plan execute against a resource holding live data). Either path avoids Terraform's own reconciliation mechanism actually destroying anything, and either path should end with a `terraform plan` showing a clean, no-change diff before considering the incident closed.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd pull up is a detailed plan output specifically to see which attribute Terraform thinks changed, because a destroy-and-recreate plan specifically means it hit something the provider treats as immutable for that resource -- so knowing exactly which attribute that is tells me whether I'm looking at 'someone changed the replication setting in the console' versus something weirder, like a provider version bump changing how an unchanged attribute gets interpreted.

To actually tell those apart, I'd go check the cloud provider's own activity log for that resource around when this first showed up -- Azure Activity Log or CloudTrail, whichever applies. If someone or some other automation actually touched that storage account outside of Terraform, it'll show up there with a timestamp and who did it. If there's genuinely nothing in the audit log, my next suspicion is a provider version bump that nobody ran a plan against at the time, because that can change how Terraform reads an attribute without the real resource having moved at all.

But regardless of which of those it turns out to be, the thing I would absolutely not do is just run apply to 'fix' it. If the plan says destroy-and-recreate, apply means exactly that -- it's going to delete the real production storage account, data included, before standing up a new one. Even if whatever drifted is completely harmless, letting Terraform execute that plan against a live production resource is not a reconciliation, it's an outage.

The actual fix depends on which way the drift should go: if the manual change is something we actually want to keep, I update the Terraform code itself to match the new reality, so the plan goes clean without ever touching the real resource. If the manual change was a mistake, I revert it directly through the cloud console or provider API, not through Terraform's destructive plan. Either way, I don't call it resolved until a fresh plan shows no diff at all.
commonMistakes: Running terraform apply on a destroy-and-recreate plan without first understanding what would actually be destroyed
Assuming all drift is malicious/accidental rather than checking for a provider-version-caused plan artifact
Not checking cloud provider audit logs to distinguish real out-of-band changes from provider behavior changes
Fixing drift by letting the destructive plan execute instead of updating code or reverting the manual change directly
Closing the incident without confirming a subsequent clean (no-diff) plan
keyPoints: A destroy-and-recreate plan signals a change to an immutable/ForceNew attribute for that resource type
Cloud provider audit/activity logs distinguish genuine out-of-band changes from provider-version plan artifacts
Never run apply on a destructive plan against a resource holding live production data to 'fix' drift
Remediation is deliberate: either update Terraform code to adopt the new reality, or revert the manual change directly
Both remediation paths avoid ever letting Terraform's destroy-and-recreate plan execute
The incident is only resolved once a fresh plan shows a clean, no-change diff

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses detailed plan output to identify the specific changed attribute
Proposes a sound method to distinguish real drift from a provider-version artifact
Correctly explains why running apply on a destructive plan is dangerous
Proposes a safe, deliberate remediation path (code update or direct revert)
Clear, accurate overall reasoning

questions.title: A Streaming MERGE Job Starts Throwing ConcurrentAppendException in Production
questions.prompt: A Databricks job that runs a streaming MERGE into a Delta table every few minutes has run reliably for months, then suddenly starts throwing ConcurrentAppendException on most runs after a second pipeline was recently granted write access to the same table for a backfill project. Diagnose the cause, explain why Delta's optimistic concurrency control did not simply 'handle' this automatically, and specify the fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
Delta Lake's optimistic concurrency control does handle many concurrent-writer scenarios automatically -- but only when the two transactions' actual file-level changes don't overlap. ConcurrentAppendException specifically means Delta detected that another transaction committed a conflicting change to the same table between when this transaction started reading and when it tried to commit, and the conflict wasn't resolvable by simply reattempting on top of the new state -- most commonly because the second writer's operation (the newly-added backfill job) is also appending to, or modifying, files in the same partition(s) the streaming MERGE's own read-set depends on, so the two operations' changes genuinely overlap at the file level, not just logically. A streaming MERGE in particular tends to be especially conflict-prone because MERGE operations read a broader footprint of existing files to evaluate the match condition (it needs to find whatever rows might match the incoming batch's keys), so its read-set is more likely to intersect with whatever partitions the new backfill job happens to be touching, compared to a simple blind append which only writes new files and rarely conflicts with another writer's appends.

The reason optimistic concurrency control doesn't just 'handle' this silently the way it does for two non-overlapping blind appends is that Delta's conflict detection is deliberately conservative about correctness: if it can't prove the two transactions' changes are independent, it has to abort one of them rather than risk silently merging two conflicting sets of changes into a corrupted result. Automatically retrying a failed MERGE without re-evaluating its match condition against the table's new post-conflict state could produce a logically wrong result (matching against stale data), so Delta surfaces the exception to the calling job rather than papering over it -- which is correct behavior, just one the pipeline's error handling wasn't built to expect because this conflict never used to happen when the streaming MERGE was the table's only writer.

The fix has two layers. Immediately, the streaming job's own retry logic needs to catch ConcurrentAppendException specifically and retry the entire micro-batch (Structured Streaming's foreachBatch-based MERGE should already be idempotent per micro-batch if written correctly, since Spark can redeliver the same micro-batch on a retry) -- most streaming frameworks and Delta-aware retry wrappers handle this if configured, but it needs to actually be configured, not assumed. Structurally, the real fix is coordinating the two writers so their operations don't collide at the partition level in the first place: scheduling the backfill job to write to a date/partition range that the streaming job's incoming data has already fully passed (so their actual file footprints never overlap), or, if genuinely concurrent writes to overlapping partitions are unavoidable, redesigning the backfill to write to a separate staging table and merging its results into the main table during a coordinated maintenance window instead of via simultaneous, uncoordinated MERGE operations against the same live table.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The timing here is the whole diagnosis -- this job ran fine for months, and it started failing right when a second pipeline got write access to the same table. ConcurrentAppendException means Delta saw a real conflict: the backfill job committed a change to files that overlapped with what the streaming MERGE needed to read to evaluate its match condition, and Delta couldn't prove the two were independent, so it aborted the MERGE rather than risk silently combining two conflicting writes into something wrong.

I'd actually point out that MERGE is more conflict-prone than a simple append specifically because of what it has to read -- it needs to scan a broader slice of existing files to figure out what matches the incoming batch, so it's much more likely to overlap with whatever partitions a second writer happens to be touching than a blind append would be, which usually just writes brand-new files and rarely steps on anyone else's read set.

And I'd be clear that Delta isn't failing to do its job here -- this is working as designed. If it can't prove the two transactions' changes are independent, silently retrying the MERGE against stale assumptions could actually produce a wrong result, so it surfaces the exception instead of guessing. The pipeline's error handling just was never built to expect this, because it never had to share the table with another concurrent writer before.

For the immediate fix, the streaming job needs retry logic that specifically catches ConcurrentAppendException and retries the whole micro-batch -- which should be safe as long as the MERGE logic in that micro-batch is actually idempotent, since Spark can redeliver the same batch. But the real fix is structural: get the backfill job scheduled or scoped so it's not touching the same partitions the streaming job is actively writing to at the same time -- either by date-range separation, or by having the backfill write to a staging table and merging it in during a coordinated window instead of fighting the streaming job for the same live partitions in real time.
commonMistakes: Assuming Delta's concurrency control should have prevented this conflict automatically in all cases
Not recognizing MERGE's broader read footprint makes it more conflict-prone than simple appends
Treating the exception as a Delta bug rather than correct, conservative conflict detection working as designed
Fixing only the retry logic without addressing the structural partition-overlap cause
Assuming an automatic retry is always safe without first confirming the MERGE logic is actually idempotent per micro-batch
keyPoints: ConcurrentAppendException means Delta detected overlapping, unresolvable file-level changes between two transactions
MERGE's broader read footprint makes it more prone to conflicts with a second concurrent writer than simple appends
Delta aborts rather than silently retrying because it cannot prove the two transactions are independent
This is correct, conservative behavior, not a bug -- the pipeline's error handling just wasn't built to expect a second writer
Immediate fix: retry logic specifically for ConcurrentAppendException, assuming idempotent micro-batch MERGE logic
Structural fix: coordinate the two writers' partition footprints or route the backfill through a staging table instead

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains ConcurrentAppendException as an overlapping-change conflict
Correctly explains why MERGE is more conflict-prone than simple appends
Correctly frames this as expected, conservative behavior rather than a bug
Proposes both immediate (retry) and structural (coordination/staging) fixes
Clear, accurate overall reasoning

questions.title: A Snowflake Warehouse's Monthly Bill Triples With No Corresponding Query Volume Increase
questions.prompt: A warehouse's Snowflake credit consumption nearly tripled month over month, but the Snowflake query history shows roughly the same number of queries as the prior month, and no new heavy workloads were onboarded. Walk through the specific things you'd check, in order, and the most likely root cause given that query count is flat but cost is not.
questions.modelAnswer:
Flat query count with tripled cost rules out 'more people are querying it' as the cause and points directly at how long the warehouse is actually running, since Snowflake bills by compute-seconds the warehouse is active, not by query count -- the same number of queries can cost very different amounts depending on how much idle time the warehouse accrues between them. The first thing I'd check is AUTO_SUSPEND configuration and actual warehouse uptime from `WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY` -- specifically whether AUTO_SUSPEND was recently changed (lengthened, or disabled entirely) or whether something is keeping the warehouse continuously 'warm' even between queries, because a warehouse sitting active and billing credits during idle gaps between a flat number of queries, instead of suspending after a short idle period and resuming on the next query, can multiply billed compute-seconds dramatically without any change in actual query workload.

Second, I'd check whether warehouse size or multi-cluster MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT changed -- someone resizing the warehouse up, or raising the max cluster count for a concurrency concern that was addressed by spinning up additional clusters that then also sit idle without suspending promptly, directly multiplies the credit rate per unit time even with identical query volume, since a larger warehouse or more running clusters cost proportionally more per second regardless of how many queries they're actually serving. Third, I'd check for a change in query mix even at flat count -- a small number of queries that got significantly more expensive (a changed query plan due to a missing/dropped clustering key, a new full-table scan replacing what used to be a pruned partition scan) can inflate total compute-seconds without changing the query count metric at all, since count doesn't capture per-query duration or data scanned.

Given the specific combination of flat query count and no new heavy workloads, the most likely single root cause is an AUTO_SUSPEND or warehouse-size/cluster-count configuration change (often an unreviewed, well-intentioned tweak -- someone raised AUTO_SUSPEND's idle timeout, or bumped MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT to fix an unrelated concurrency complaint) that increased idle billed time or per-second cost rate, rather than anything about the actual queries themselves -- which is exactly why reviewing `WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY` and the warehouse's current configuration against its configuration a month ago, not the query history, is the fastest path to the actual root cause.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing that stands out to me is that query count didn't move but cost did -- that rules out 'we're just querying it more' and points straight at how the warehouse is being billed, which in Snowflake is by compute-seconds it's actually running, not by how many queries you ran. So the same 50,000 queries this month and last month can cost wildly different amounts depending on how much idle time got billed in between them.

First thing I'd pull up is WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY alongside the warehouse's AUTO_SUSPEND setting, and specifically check whether that setting got changed recently -- lengthened, or turned off entirely. If something's keeping the warehouse warm between queries instead of suspending quickly and resuming on demand, you can triple your billed time without a single extra query ever running.

Second, I'd check whether the warehouse size or the multi-cluster max count changed. If someone bumped the size up, or raised MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT to deal with some concurrency complaint, and those extra clusters aren't suspending promptly either, that's a direct multiplier on cost per second with zero change to query volume.

Third, I'd look at whether a handful of queries quietly got more expensive even though the count is flat -- something like a dropped clustering key causing what used to be a pruned scan to become a full-table scan. Query count doesn't capture that at all, only duration and bytes scanned would show it.

But given that there's no new heavy workload and the count is genuinely flat, my first bet is a config change -- AUTO_SUSPEND or cluster count -- that nobody flagged as cost-relevant at the time. I'd check the warehouse's current config against what it looked like a month ago before I'd even start digging into individual query plans.
commonMistakes: Assuming flat query count rules out a billing-relevant change and looking only at query logic
Not checking AUTO_SUSPEND configuration and actual uptime via WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY
Not checking whether warehouse size or MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT changed recently
Assuming cost scales linearly with query count rather than with billed compute-seconds
Not comparing current warehouse configuration against its configuration from before the cost increase
keyPoints: Snowflake bills by compute-seconds the warehouse runs, not by query count, so flat count does not mean flat cost
AUTO_SUSPEND changes (or being disabled) can dramatically increase billed idle time between queries
Warehouse size or MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT increases multiply cost per second independent of query volume
A small number of queries becoming more expensive (e.g., lost pruning) can inflate cost at flat query count
WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY and current-vs-prior configuration comparison are the fastest diagnostic path
The most likely root cause here is an unreviewed AUTO_SUSPEND or sizing/cluster-count configuration change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons that billing is by compute-seconds, not query count
Correctly identifies AUTO_SUSPEND/uptime as the primary suspect to check
Correctly identifies warehouse size/cluster count changes as a contributing factor
Mentions per-query cost changes (e.g., lost pruning) as a secondary possibility
Clear, accurate overall diagnostic ordering

questions.title: A Fabric Capacity Incident: Diagnosing Sudden Rejection After Weeks of Carry-Forward
questions.prompt: A Fabric capacity that has run fine for a year suddenly starts rejecting new interactive queries outright, with no single large job obviously to blame. The Capacity Metrics app shows utilization has been hovering just over 100% for the past three weeks. Diagnose what actually happened leading up to this incident, why it looked fine until it suddenly didn't, and what the remediation plan should include both immediately and structurally.
questions.modelAnswer:
Three weeks of utilization hovering just over 100% is the key detail: that's exactly the carry-forward regime, where Fabric keeps letting new operations run but pushes their cost forward onto future capacity rather than rejecting them outright, as long as utilization stays in a moderate overage band. For three weeks, the capacity was quietly accumulating a debt of carried-forward compute cost that never fully got paid down, because whatever was driving utilization above 100% was either continuous or recurring often enough that the capacity never had a clean low-utilization stretch to absorb the backlog. That's why 'it looked fine' for three weeks -- carry-forward is specifically designed to keep things running smoothly from the user's perspective during moderate, temporary overage, so interactive queries kept succeeding the whole time, with the growing debt invisible to anyone just checking 'are my reports loading.'

Rejection kicks in once that accumulated overage crosses a higher threshold or persists long enough that Fabric's throttling policy escalates past what carry-forward alone can absorb -- so the sudden rejection isn't really sudden at all, it's the visible endpoint of three weeks of invisible debt finally crossing the line where the capacity's throttling policy stops lending against future capacity and starts refusing new work outright. The lack of one single large job to blame is consistent with this: carry-forward overage can accumulate from many moderately-oversized recurring jobs (several dataflow refreshes, a handful of Spark notebooks, routine report usage) that each individually look unremarkable, but collectively exceed capacity consistently enough, day after day, that the debt never clears.

The immediate remediation is to find and pause or reschedule whatever load is recurring most consistently during the hours utilization is highest -- using the Capacity Metrics app's per-item breakdown, not the aggregate, to identify specific background jobs and their typical run times -- to let the capacity actually drop below 100% for a sustained period and pay down the carried-forward debt, since simply waiting it out while new load keeps arriving at the same rate won't resolve it. Structurally, the remediation should include: setting up proactive alerting on sustained utilization above some threshold (e.g., 80-90%) well before it reaches the carry-forward-to-rejection boundary, rather than only noticing via a hard rejection incident; reviewing whether the capacity's SKU is genuinely sized for its actual sustained load rather than just its average load; and considering splitting consistently heavy workloads (a particularly large recurring Spark job, a high-frequency Eventstream) onto a separate capacity so one team's growth doesn't silently consume headroom the whole shared capacity needed.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The three weeks of hovering just over 100% is actually the whole story here -- that's the carry-forward zone, where Fabric doesn't reject anything yet, it just quietly pushes the cost of whatever's running over onto future capacity. For three weeks, this capacity was running a debt that never got paid off, because utilization never dropped low enough for long enough to absorb it. And carry-forward is specifically designed to make that invisible from a user's perspective -- reports were loading fine the whole time, which is exactly why nobody noticed anything was wrong until it suddenly wasn't fine anymore.

The rejection wasn't really sudden -- it's just the moment that three weeks of accumulated debt finally crossed whatever threshold makes Fabric stop lending against future capacity and start saying no outright. And I wouldn't expect one obvious culprit job here, because this kind of slow-building overage usually comes from several moderately-oversized recurring things -- a handful of dataflow refreshes, a couple of notebooks, normal report traffic -- that each look fine individually but together are consistently a bit too much, day after day, for three weeks straight.

For the immediate fix, I'd go into the per-item breakdown in the Capacity Metrics app -- not the aggregate chart, that's what hid this in the first place -- and find whatever's running most consistently during peak hours, and pause or reschedule enough of it that utilization actually drops below 100% for a real stretch, long enough to pay down that carried-forward debt. Just waiting for it to clear on its own won't work if new load keeps arriving at the same rate.

And structurally, I'd put in alerting on sustained utilization well before the rejection threshold -- 80 or 90 percent sustained for days, not just a momentary spike -- so this gets caught as a trend next time, not as an outage. I'd also push to review whether this capacity is actually sized for its real sustained load, and consider splitting off whatever's consistently heaviest onto its own capacity so it's not quietly eating headroom the rest of the workload needs.
commonMistakes: Treating the rejection as a sudden, unexplained event rather than the endpoint of weeks of accumulating carry-forward debt
Looking for one single large job to blame instead of several moderately-oversized recurring workloads
Trying to fix it by waiting it out rather than actively reducing load to pay down the debt
Using the aggregate utilization chart instead of the per-item breakdown to find the actual contributors
Not implementing proactive alerting on sustained utilization well before the rejection threshold
keyPoints: Sustained utilization just over 100% for weeks is the carry-forward regime, which masks problems from users
Carry-forward debt accumulates invisibly because interactive queries keep succeeding during that period
Rejection is the visible endpoint of accumulated debt crossing a throttling escalation threshold, not a sudden event
Multiple moderately-oversized recurring jobs, not one obvious culprit, typically drive this pattern
Immediate fix requires actively reducing load (via per-item breakdown) to pay down the debt, not waiting
Structural fix includes proactive sustained-utilization alerting and reviewing SKU sizing against real sustained load

Correctly explains why the problem was invisible until rejection occurred
Correctly reasons about multiple moderate contributors rather than one culprit

questions.title: A Bad Merge to Main Breaks Production dbt Builds: Rollback Strategy Under Pressure
questions.prompt: A PR merged to main an hour ago, and production dbt runs have started failing downstream. The original author is unreachable for the next few hours. Walk through your actual rollback decision process -- revert-the-merge-commit versus hotfix-forward -- the git mechanics of doing it safely, and how you'd communicate the incident while you work, given that branch protection requires PR review before merging to main.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first decision is revert-the-merge versus hotfix-forward, and the deciding factor is whether the fix is actually known and small, or whether understanding the failure well enough to craft a safe fix will itself take real time. If the breaking change is narrow and the fix is obvious (a typo in a ref(), a wrong column name) and I can verify it quickly, a targeted hotfix PR is often faster and less disruptive than a full revert, especially if other unrelated work has also merged to main since the breaking PR and a full revert would also roll back that unrelated work. If the breaking change touched something more structural, or I can't be confident I understand the full blast radius within a few minutes, reverting is the safer default -- it's mechanical, well-understood, and gets production back to a known-good state immediately while leaving time to properly diagnose and re-attempt the original change later, rather than rushing a second risky change on top of an already-broken state under pressure.

Mechanically, `git revert -m 1 <merge-commit-sha>` (the `-m 1` specifying which parent to revert against, since a merge commit has two parents) creates a new commit that undoes exactly the merge commit's changes without rewriting history -- this is the key reason to revert rather than force-push main back to an earlier commit: force-pushing main rewrites shared history, which is both generally disallowed by branch protection and genuinely dangerous if anyone else has already pulled or branched from the commits being removed. A revert commit is a normal, additive commit, so it goes through the exact same PR-and-review branch-protection process as any other change to main -- which matters here, because even an incident rollback shouldn't bypass review entirely; getting a second engineer to quickly eyeball the revert PR (even a fast, five-minute review) catches the case where the revert itself has an unexpected interaction with something that merged after the original breaking PR.

Communication should happen in parallel with, not after, the technical work: posting in an incident channel immediately with what's known (production dbt builds failing since roughly X time, suspected cause is PR #N merged at Y time, original author unreachable, rollback in progress) lets anyone else who might be independently investigating the same symptom stop duplicating effort, and sets expectations for stakeholders waiting on downstream data without them needing to ask. Once the revert PR is reviewed and merged, a brief follow-up noting production is restored and that a full postmortem/retry of the original change will follow closes the loop, and the original PR's author should be looped in asynchronously as soon as they're reachable, both to understand what went wrong and to ensure the revert doesn't quietly block their actual intended change forever.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first call I'd make is revert versus hotfix, and honestly it comes down to how confident I am, right now, in a fix. If it's something small and obvious -- a wrong column reference, a typo -- and I can verify the fix quickly, I'd rather ship a targeted hotfix than a full revert, especially if other unrelated work has also landed on main since the breaking PR, because a revert would roll that back too. But if I'm not fully confident I understand the blast radius in the next few minutes, I default to reverting -- it's mechanical, it's well understood, and it gets production back to a known-good state immediately instead of me trying to craft a correct fix under pressure with the original author unreachable to sanity-check my understanding of what they were trying to do.

Mechanically, I'd use git revert with -m 1 against the merge commit's SHA, not a force-push to roll main back. A revert is a normal new commit that undoes the change -- it doesn't rewrite history, so it doesn't break anything for anyone who already pulled those commits, and it goes through the exact same PR process as any other change, which actually matters here. Even in an incident, I want someone else's quick eyes on the revert PR before it merges -- a five-minute review can catch something like 'wait, a later PR actually built on top of that change,' which would make a straight revert more complicated than expected.

And I'd be posting updates the whole time this is happening, not after. As soon as I suspect the cause, I'd put in an incident channel exactly what's known -- which PR, when it merged, what's failing, that the original author's unreachable, and that a revert is in progress -- so nobody else duplicates the investigation and stakeholders waiting on data know what's happening without having to ask. Once it's merged and production's confirmed healthy again, a short follow-up closes the loop, and I'd make sure the original author gets looped in as soon as they're back, both to actually fix the underlying thing right and to make sure my revert isn't accidentally blocking real work they still need to land.
commonMistakes: Force-pushing main to an earlier commit instead of using a proper revert commit
Bypassing branch protection/review entirely for the rollback, even under incident pressure
Defaulting to a rushed hotfix under pressure without being genuinely confident in its correctness and scope
Reverting the merge commit without specifying the correct parent (-m 1) on a two-parent merge commit
Delaying incident communication until after the fix is complete instead of communicating in parallel
keyPoints: Choose hotfix-forward only when the fix is small, well-understood, and quickly verifiable; otherwise default to revert
git revert -m 1 against the merge commit SHA safely undoes the change without rewriting shared history
Never force-push main to roll back; it rewrites history and endangers anyone who already pulled the removed commits
The revert PR should still go through branch-protection review, even on an expedited basis
Communicate what's known in an incident channel immediately and in parallel with the technical fix
Loop in the original author asynchronously once reachable, both for root cause and to unblock their real change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the revert-vs-hotfix decision criteria
Correctly specifies safe git revert mechanics (not force-push) respecting branch protection
Proposes still obtaining expedited review on the revert PR
Describes sound parallel incident communication
Clear, accurate overall reasoning

questions.title: A Databricks Multi-Workspace Metastore Starts Exposing Masked Columns Unmasked
questions.prompt: A company recently attached a new, third workspace to its shared Unity Catalog metastore. Shortly after, an analyst in that new workspace reports they can see unmasked PII in a column that's supposed to be protected by a column-masking policy that's worked correctly in the other two workspaces for months. Diagnose the likely cause given the multi-workspace topology, and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
Column masking policies in Unity Catalog typically apply conditionally -- a masking function is usually written to check the querying user's group membership or role (e.g., unmask only if the user belongs to a 'pii_access' group) rather than unconditionally masking for everyone, and that conditional logic evaluates correctly in the two original workspaces specifically because whatever group/role mapping the masking function depends on was already correctly configured and tested there. The most likely cause in a newly-attached third workspace is that the masking policy's underlying group-membership check is evaluating against a group that either doesn't exist the same way in the new workspace's context, resolves differently, or -- more subtly -- that the new workspace was given broader default access during onboarding (e.g., its default access connector or a broadly-scoped service principal was accidentally added to the 'pii_access' group during setup, intending something else entirely) than the original two workspaces ever had.

Another common root cause specific to multi-workspace metastore topology: if the masking function itself references account-level or metastore-level group objects, but the new workspace has a workspace-local group with a colliding or similar name that's being resolved instead of the intended account-level group (a namespace collision between workspace-local and account-level identities), the masking check can silently evaluate against the wrong group definition in the new workspace's context even though the exact same policy SQL is attached to the exact same table across all three workspaces. This is specifically a multi-workspace governance gotcha: a masking policy's SQL doesn't change at all between workspaces since it's a Unity Catalog object shared via the common metastore, but what that SQL's group-membership check actually resolves to at query time can differ by workspace if the user/group identity resolution isn't as centralized as the table-level policy object itself.

The fix starts with auditing exactly which users/service-principals are in whatever group the masking function checks, specifically from the new workspace's perspective (not just checking the group's members in the Unity Catalog account console, but confirming how that analyst's session actually resolves their effective group membership when querying from that workspace) -- if the new workspace's onboarding added the wrong principal to the sensitive group, remove it immediately and treat it as an access incident requiring a review of who else may have queried that column unmasked since the new workspace was attached. If it's the namespace-collision scenario, the fix is renaming or fully qualifying the group reference in the masking function to unambiguously point at the correct account-level group object, and then auditing every workspace attached to the metastore to confirm no other workspace has the same collision risk.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first assumption is that the masking policy's SQL itself hasn't changed -- it's a Unity Catalog object shared through the one metastore, so the same policy is genuinely attached to that column in all three workspaces. What's different is almost certainly how the masking function's group-membership check resolves in this new workspace specifically. Most masking policies aren't unconditional -- they check something like 'is this user in the pii_access group' and only unmask for members, and that check has worked correctly in the original two workspaces because whatever group mapping it depends on was set up and tested there months ago.

So the first thing I'd check is exactly who's actually in that pii_access group from this new workspace's point of view -- not just glancing at the group's member list in the account console, but confirming how this specific analyst's access resolves when they query from this workspace. A really common onboarding mistake is a service principal or a broad default-access group getting added to something like pii_access accidentally during new-workspace setup, when the intent was something totally unrelated.

The other thing I'd specifically check for, because it's a genuine multi-workspace gotcha, is a naming collision -- if there's a workspace-local group with a name similar to the account-level group the masking function is supposed to check, and the new workspace happens to resolve to the local one instead of the intended account-level one, you get exactly this symptom: identical policy SQL, different real-world behavior, purely because of which group object actually gets resolved in that workspace's context.

Once I find which of those it is, the fix is either removing the wrongly-added principal from the sensitive group immediately, or fully qualifying the group reference in the masking function so there's no ambiguity about which group object it means -- and either way, I'd treat this as a real access incident and go check whether that analyst, or anyone else in the new workspace, already queried that column unmasked since it was attached.
commonMistakes: Assuming the masking policy's SQL itself must be different per workspace when it is a shared metastore object
Not checking the actual effective group-membership resolution from the specific workspace's query context
Overlooking onboarding-time group misconfiguration (overly broad default access granted to the new workspace)
Not considering workspace-local vs. account-level group naming collisions as a root cause
Not treating the discovery as a retroactive access incident requiring an audit of who already queried the data
keyPoints: Masking policies are usually conditional on a group-membership check, not an unconditional mask
The policy SQL is shared via the metastore and identical across workspaces; the group resolution can differ
Likely causes: onboarding misconfiguration adding the wrong principal to the sensitive group, or a group naming collision
Diagnosis requires checking effective group resolution specifically from the new workspace's context
Fix is removing the wrongly-granted access or fully qualifying the group reference to avoid ambiguity
This should be treated as a retroactive access incident, auditing who already saw unmasked data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies conditional group-membership-based masking as the relevant mechanism
Correctly reasons that policy SQL is shared while group resolution can differ per workspace
Identifies at least one specific plausible root cause (onboarding misconfig or naming collision)
Proposes a concrete diagnostic and fix
Treats this as an access incident requiring audit

questions.title: A Prompt-Injection Attempt Against a Cortex-Style Data Agent Reading Untrusted Content
questions.prompt: A support team built an AI agent on top of Snowflake Cortex that reads customer support tickets (free-text, customer-authored) and uses tool calls to query account data and draft responses. During a review, a security engineer finds a ticket where the customer wrote text designed to make the agent ignore its instructions and dump another customer's account data. Diagnose why this attack works structurally against this kind of agent, and specify concrete governance/architecture controls that actually mitigate it -- not just a prompt-level instruction telling the model to 'ignore instructions in user content.'
questions.modelAnswer:
The attack works structurally because an LLM-based agent has no reliable, architectural way to distinguish 'instructions from the system/developer' from 'instructions embedded in content it's reading,' once both are present in the same context window -- the model processes tokens, and tokens that look like instructions get weighted similarly regardless of whether they came from the system prompt or from a customer's free-text ticket. Telling the model in its system prompt to 'ignore any instructions found in user content' is a mitigation at the same unreliable layer as the attack itself -- it raises the bar slightly but is not a dependable control, because a sufficiently creative injection can be phrased to specifically target and override that very instruction (e.g., claiming to be a system message, or layering misdirection), and there's no proof-of-correctness guarantee that a given phrasing will always fail against the model's actual behavior.

The controls that actually mitigate this live outside the prompt, at the tool-call and data-access layer, because that's the layer that can be enforced deterministically rather than probabilistically. First: the agent's tool-calling layer should never grant the LLM's tool calls more data access than the specific authenticated end user (the support agent operating the tool, or the ticket's own associated customer) is independently entitled to see -- if the agent is answering on behalf of customer A's ticket, its underlying account-data query tool should be scoped (via row-level security, a parameterized query bound to that ticket's own customer_id, or a dedicated service role with narrowly scoped grants) so that it is structurally incapable of returning customer B's data, regardless of what the LLM decides to ask for based on injected instructions. The LLM choosing to call a tool with the 'wrong' customer_id as an argument should fail at the data layer, not succeed and then rely on the LLM having correctly refused.

Second, any tool call that would access or disclose sensitive account data should go through policy enforcement that doesn't trust the LLM's own tool-call arguments as authoritative -- validating that the customer_id argument the model passes actually matches the customer_id associated with the ticket/session context the agent is legitimately operating within, rejecting the call outright if it doesn't match, independent of why the model generated that argument. Third, logging and anomaly detection on tool-call patterns (an agent suddenly requesting a different customer's data than the one associated with its current session) gives a detection layer even if a novel injection technique gets past the first two controls. The governing principle is: never rely on the model reliably refusing a malicious instruction as the actual security boundary; the security boundary has to be enforced by code and access controls the model cannot talk its way around, with prompt-level instructions treated as, at best, a weak additional layer, not the control itself.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The reason this attack works at all is that the model doesn't have a reliable, built-in way to tell 'this is a real instruction from us, the people who built this agent' apart from 'this is text in a customer ticket that happens to be phrased like an instruction.' Once both end up in the same context, they're just tokens to the model, and a cleverly worded injection can absolutely get weighted as if it were a legitimate instruction. So telling the model in the system prompt 'ignore instructions you find in user content' is a start, but it's fighting the attack on the attack's own turf -- it's still just more text the model has to correctly interpret and prioritize, and a good enough injection can specifically target that exact instruction and try to talk the model out of following it.

The actual fix has to live below the model, at the layer that doesn't care what the model 'decided.' The biggest one: the tool the agent calls to pull account data should be scoped so it's physically incapable of returning anyone's data except the customer tied to the ticket it's currently working -- through row-level security, a parameterized query bound to that ticket's own customer ID, whatever the mechanism, but enforced at the data layer, not by trusting the model to only ask for the right customer. If the model gets talked into trying to request customer B's data while working customer A's ticket, that request should just fail at the database, full stop, regardless of why the model asked for it.

On top of that, I'd have the tool-calling layer independently validate that whatever customer ID the model passes as an argument actually matches the session or ticket context the agent is legitimately operating in, and reject the call if it doesn't match -- not trusting the model's own arguments as authoritative. And I'd log every tool call with its arguments so an anomaly like 'this session suddenly asked for a different customer's data' gets flagged even if some future injection technique gets past everything else. The real principle here is: the model refusing the bad instruction is a nice-to-have, not the security boundary. The actual boundary has to be something code enforces that the model literally cannot argue its way around.
commonMistakes: Treating a system-prompt instruction to ignore injected content as a sufficient security control
Not distinguishing prompt-level mitigations (probabilistic, bypassable) from access-layer controls (deterministic, enforceable)
Trusting the LLM's own tool-call arguments as authoritative for data access scope
Not scoping the underlying data-access tool to the specific authenticated session/ticket context
Omitting logging/anomaly detection on tool-call patterns as a defense-in-depth layer
keyPoints: LLMs cannot reliably distinguish system instructions from instructions embedded in untrusted content they read
Prompt-level 'ignore injected instructions' guidance is a weak, bypassable mitigation, not a real security boundary
The real control scopes the underlying data-access tool so it cannot return data beyond what the session/ticket legitimately permits
Tool-call arguments from the model must be independently validated against session context, never trusted as authoritative
Logging and anomaly detection on tool-call patterns provide defense-in-depth against novel injection techniques
Security boundaries must be enforced by code/access controls the model cannot talk its way around

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why the model cannot reliably distinguish injected instructions
Correctly identifies prompt-level mitigation as insufficient on its own
Proposes concrete data-layer access scoping as the real control
Proposes independent validation of tool-call arguments against session context
Mentions logging/anomaly detection as defense-in-depth

questions.title: Build vs. Buy: Designing a Change-Data-Capture Layer for 40 Operational Databases
questions.prompt: A mid-size retailer needs change-data-capture from 40 operational databases (a mix of SQL Server, Postgres, and MySQL) into its lakehouse, within 5 minutes of latency, with a small (4-person) data platform team. Walk through how you'd approach the build-vs-buy decision -- what specifically building your own CDC layer would require that a managed tool (Fivetran, Debezium-on-your-own-infra, Airbyte) would not, and what you'd actually recommend and why.
questions.modelAnswer:
Building a CDC layer from scratch across three different source database engines means the team is signing up to build and maintain, per engine, a correct log-reading mechanism (SQL Server CDC/CT or transaction log reading, Postgres logical replication slots and WAL parsing, MySQL binlog parsing), schema-change detection and propagation, exactly-once or at-least-once delivery semantics with deduplication downstream, connector-level monitoring and alerting, and backfill/resync tooling for whenever a connector falls behind or a source schema changes in a way the connector can't auto-handle. Each of those is a real distributed-systems problem with sharp edges (binlog rotation during an outage, replication slot WAL buildup if a consumer falls behind, handling DDL changes mid-stream), and getting all three engines' versions of these problems right, and keeping them right as each engine's own versions evolve, is a multi-engineer, multi-quarter commitment even before onboarding the first of 40 actual databases.

For a 4-person platform team, that's the deciding factor: a managed CDC tool (Fivetran, Airbyte, or a well-operated Debezium-on-managed-Kafka-Connect setup) has already solved the hard, narrow, and non-differentiating parts of this problem -- log parsing correctness per engine, schema drift handling, connector health monitoring -- and selling/offering that as the product is literally their core competency, which a 4-person team moonlighting on CDC internals on top of their other platform responsibilities cannot realistically match in reliability within any reasonable timeframe.
